chapters.title: Book I
paragraphs: After seven years of wandering, the Trojans set sail for Italy but are overtaken by a terrible storm that Aeolus raises at Juno's request. The storm sinks one ship and scatters the rest. Neptune drives off the winds and calms the sea. Aeneas, with his own ship and six others, reaches an African port safely. Venus complains to Jupiter about her son's misfortunes. Jupiter comforts her and sends Mercury to ensure a kind welcome among the Carthaginians. Aeneas goes out to explore the country and meets his mother disguised as a huntress, who leads him unseen to Carthage. There he finds his friends whom he thought lost, and receives a warm welcome from Queen Dido. Through Venus's scheming, Dido begins to fall in love with him. After hearing some of his story, she asks him to tell the full history of his adventures since the fall of Troy, which fills the next two books.

I sing of arms and the man who, driven by fate and Juno's relentless hatred, was forced into exile from the shores of Troy. He endured long hardships on both sea and land. Before he could win the realm of Latium and build the city destined by the gods, he suffered through uncertain war. He restored his banished gods to their rightful worship and established a sure line of succession. From this line came the Alban fathers and the long glories of majestic Rome. O Muse, tell me the causes and the crimes. What goddess was offended, and why did she hate this brave and righteous man so bitterly? Why did the Queen of Heaven torment him with endless troubles and drive him into war? Can heavenly minds hold such fierce resentment, or take such spite in mortal suffering?

Far from the mouth of the Tiber, across the sea, stood an ancient city: Carthage, a Tyrian colony. Its people were fierce in war and devoted to trade. Juno loved this city above all others, more than her own Argos or Samos. Here she kept her chariot. Here, if heaven allowed, she hoped to establish the seat of a mighty empire. Yet she had heard an ancient prophecy, long spoken among the gods, that one day the Trojan race would destroy Carthage and tear down its towers. Not only that, but they would rise to rule over all the nations of the earth. She brooded on this, fearing it was fated to happen. She could not forget the war she had waged against Troy on behalf of her beloved Greeks. Deep in her heart, old grudges still burned: the judgment of Paris, who had scorned her beauty; the honor bestowed on the stolen Ganymede; and the glory of Electra's line, which wounded her pride. Each slight was cause enough on its own, and all combined to fuel her haughty rage. For these reasons, she drove the remnants of the Trojan people far from the Latin coast. For seven long years, the unhappy wanderers were tossed by storms across the sea. Such was the cost, such the labor required to found the Roman name.

The Trojan fleet had barely left the shores of Sicily behind, with sails unfurled and oars churning the sea with cheerful shouts. But Juno, still seething with endless resentment, gave voice to her fury.

"Am I defeated then? Must I give in?" she cried. "Must the Trojans rule in Italy? So Fate demands, and Jupiter enforces it. My power cannot turn them from their course. Yet Athena, burning with spite, could set the Greek fleet ablaze and drown its men, all for the offense of one. She dared to throw Jupiter's own thunderbolts. She tossed ships with whirlwinds from below, exposed the depths of the sea, and pinned the wretch Ajax to a rock with lightning still burning in his chest. But I, who walk in majesty above as the sister and wife of Jupiter, have spent years waging war against the thin remains of ruined Troy. What nation will worship Juno now, or lay offerings on my neglected altars?"

Blazing with rage, the goddess made her way to the land of storms. In a vast cave of living rock, the tyrant Aeolus sat on his throne, using his imperial power to restrain the struggling winds. He kept thundering tempests locked in dark prisons. The restless captives strained this way and that, pressing for release until the mountains groaned. High in his hall, the fearless king stood with his scepter, commanding their rage. Without his control, their unchecked fury would sweep earth, air, and sea through empty space, and heaven itself would fly before the driving gale. Fearing this, the Father of the Gods had confined their fury to those dark caverns, weighed down by mountains. He set a king over them with authority to loose their chains or hold them back. To this king, Juno now addressed her plea.

"Aeolus, the King of Heaven has given you power over tempests and winds. Your force alone can restrain their fury, or smooth the waves, or swell the troubled sea. A race of wandering exiles I despise is crossing the Tuscan sea with fair winds, bound for fruitful Italy. There they plan to set up new temples for their conquered gods. Raise all your winds! Shroud the skies in night! Sink or scatter my enemies! I have fourteen beautiful sea nymphs in my train. The fairest of them, Deiopeia, shall be yours. Grant my wish, and she will be your bride, the mother of a noble line."

The god replied: "It is yours to command, my queen, and my duty to obey. Everything I have, this airy kingdom and this wide authority, is a gift from your generous hand. Through your favor I sit at Jupiter's table among the gods. You give me power over storms and tempests. I hold my empire from you."

He spoke, and drove his quivering spear against the mountainside. The winds rushed through the gaping wound, dancing high in the air and sweeping across the ground. They settled on the sea and churned it into chaos. South, East, and West winds roared together, rolling foaming waves toward the shore. Cables snapped. Sailors screamed in terror. Black night swallowed the sky, and heaven itself vanished from sight. Thunder crashed from pole to pole. Lightning split the darkness with brief, blinding flashes. Everything bore the image of death in its many forms. Aeneas, the Trojan chief, stood frozen with fear. Lifting his hands and eyes to heaven, he cried out: "Three and four times blessed are those who died beneath the walls of Troy, in their parents' sight! O Diomedes, bravest of the Greeks, why could I not have fallen by your strong arm and lain on the plains of Troy beside noble Hector, or great Sarpedon, where the river Simois carried shields and helmets and the bodies of heroes in its current?"

While the prince lamented his fate, a fierce north wind tore into his sails and shattered them. The towering waves hurled the ships toward the sky. Oars splintered under the force. The galleys turned broadside to the sea. Through gaping waves, the crews stared down into the boiling deep. Three ships were driven south and dashed onto hidden reefs the Italian sailors called the Altars, barely visible above the waterline. Three more were seized by the east wind and dragged onto shallow sandbars, stranded in mid-ocean. The ship of Orontes, carrying the Lycian crew, was struck before Aeneas's eyes by a towering wave. The pilot was torn from the rudder and hurled headlong. Three times the ship spun around, then split apart and sank. Here and there, arms, treasure, and men floated on the waves. The stoutest remaining vessels gave way to the storm. Water poured through loosened planks. The ships of Ilioneus, old Alethes, faithful Achates, and young bold Abas all suffered the same fate, their seams gaping as the sea rushed in.

Meanwhile, imperial Neptune heard the roar of breaking waves and grew alarmed for his watery realm. He raised his majestic head above the surface, calm and serene, and surveyed earth, sea, and sky. He saw the Trojan fleet scattered and distressed, overwhelmed by storm and flood. He knew at once his sister Juno's jealous schemes. He summoned the East and West winds and fixed them with a furious glare. "How dare you?" he thundered. "Where do you get this insolence, to ravage sea and land without my command? To raise such mountains of water? First let me calm these waves, and then you will answer for this. Go tell your master that the seas and the trident are mine, not his. His power extends only to his hollow caverns. Let him be king there, the jailer of the wind, and bluster in his empty hall." Even as he spoke, he smoothed the sea, scattered the clouds, and brought back the sun. Sea nymphs pushed the ships free of the rocks. Neptune himself opened passages through the sandbars with his trident. As when a grave and respected man appears before a rioting mob and calms them with sober words, quenching their rage, so the Father of the Flood calmed the waters. He rode his chariot high over the gentle waves and restored peace to the sea. The weary Trojans pulled at their battered oars and made for the nearest Libyan shore.

There lay a sheltered bay, screened from the open sea by an island that broke the waves on either side. Between two rows of towering rocks, a wooded hillside rose above, with groves of evergreen. Below the overhanging cliff, a grotto with mossy seats offered rest from the heat. Crystal streams trickled through the living rock. No ropes or anchors were needed here, for no storms could reach this place. Seven ships found shelter in this happy harbor, the thin remnants of the scattered fleet. The Trojans, worn out with hardship, leaped ashore and stretched themselves gratefully on the sand.

First, good Achates struck flint against flint to coax out a spark. He caught the tiny flame in a bed of dry leaves and fed it with kindling until it blazed high. The Trojans, dripping wet, gathered around the cheerful fire. Some dried their salt-stained grain, then ground it between stones and prepared to eat. Aeneas climbed the cliff above to search the sea for any sign of his missing ships. He saw no vessels anywhere, but spotted three great stags leading a herd across the plain below. He seized Achates' bow and quiver. He brought down the lead stags first, then the rest of the herd, and did not stop until seven mighty animals lay on the ground, one for each ship. He carried them back to the port and divided the meat in equal shares. Then he opened the jars of wine that generous Acestes had given them when they left Sicily. He shared it out and spoke to ease his people's grief. "My friends, endure. Be brave. Jupiter will bring our suffering to a good end. You have faced the rocks of Scylla and the cave of the Cyclops. What worse can come? Take courage and put aside your fear. The day will come when you will look back on these sorrows with pleasure. Through all these dangers, we press on toward Latium, where the fates have promised us a home. There the kingdom of Troy will rise again. Endure this hardship, and save yourselves for better days."

He spoke these words, but they did not come from his heart. Behind his confident smile, he hid his deep anxiety. His companions, putting aside their worries, set to work on the feast. They skinned the deer, cut up the meat, and boiled the still-trembling joints in cauldrons while others roasted the entrails on spits over the fire. Stretched out on the grass, they ate their fill and drank their wine. When hunger was satisfied, their talk turned to their absent friends. They wavered between hope and dread, wondering whether those companions were alive or dead. Aeneas grieved most of all for brave Orontes and for the uncertain fate of Gyas, Lycus, and Amycus. The day ended, but their sorrows did not.

From on high, almighty Jupiter surveyed the earth, the air, the shores, and the seas. At last, his gaze settled on the Libyan coast. As he pondered the miseries of humankind, Venus appeared before him with lowered eyes, not free from tears, and spoke to her heavenly father.

"O King of Gods and Men, whose mighty hand hurls thunder across sea and land, ruling all with absolute power: how has my faithful son offended you? What crime has vanished Troy committed? After losing all hope of Italy, tossed by storms across every sea and shut out from every shore, this is how you repay them? You once promised that from the Trojan line would come a divine race of Romans who would hold the world in awe and give law to every land and ocean. How has your decree been reversed? When Troy fell, I comforted myself by weighing fate against fate. But now the same fortune still pursues these wretched survivors. What end to their suffering have you decreed, great king? Antenor escaped through the Greek army, sailed safely to Illyria, and founded Padua, where his Trojans live in peace. But we, your own descendants, entitled to heaven's protection, have lost our ships and been betrayed. For the anger of one goddess, we are kept from Latium and the throne you promised. Are these the rewards you give? Is this how Jupiter keeps his word?"
The Father of the immortal race smiled at her with that serene, gentle look he wears when he clears the skies. He kissed his daughter tenderly and replied.

"My daughter, do not be afraid. The fates of your people stand firm and unchanged. You will see the walls of Lavinium as promised. When fate calls Aeneas, you will carry him up to heaven. No decree of mine has been reversed. Let me ease your worry and reveal what the scrolls of fate contain. Your son will wage victorious war in Italy, tame fierce nations, build cities, and establish laws. After three years of ruling in Latium, his son Ascanius, now called Iulus, will begin his own reign. For thirty years he will wear the crown, then move the capital to Alba Longa. There, for three hundred years, the Trojan dynasty will rule. Then Ilia, a royal priestess pregnant by Mars, will bear twin boys. Romulus, nursed by a she-wolf, will found his city, call its people Romans and the city Rome. For them, I set no boundaries of empire and no limits of time. I grant them rule without end. Even stubborn Juno, who now torments earth, sea, and heaven, will relent and join me in cherishing the Trojan line. The conquered world will bow to Rome, the nation of the toga. In the fullness of time, the Julian line will produce Caesar, whose empire the ocean will bound and whose fame the stars will celebrate. Then cruel war will cease. The stern age will soften into peace. Faith will return, and the dreadful gates of War will be sealed shut, with Fury chained inside."

Jupiter spoke, and sent Mercury down with orders to open the ports of Carthage to the Trojan guests. The god feared that Dido, not knowing the will of fate, might drive them from her land. Mercury flew down from heaven, carried out his mission, and displayed his divine staff. The grumbling of the Carthaginian people ceased. As the fates required, they offered peace. Queen Dido herself set aside her harsh laws and took pity on the Trojan cause.

Meanwhile, Aeneas lay awake through the dark night, his mind seized by anxiety. But when the sun brought back the cheerful day, he rose to explore the coast. Beneath a cliff, he hid his ships. Then, armed with two spears and accompanied only by faithful Achates, he set out. Deep in the woods, his goddess mother appeared before him. She was disguised as a huntress, her knees bare, her dress tied up in knots, her hair loose in the wind, carrying a bow with a quiver at her back. She looked like a Spartan maiden. "Have you seen one of my sisters?" she asked. "She was chasing a boar through these woods, dressed like me, with a spotted lynx-skin and a painted quiver."

Aeneas replied: "I have seen no one of your company, maiden, or whatever name suits you best, for you seem more than mortal. Your voice and bearing reveal a divine nature. If you are Diana's sister, or one of the nymphs, be kind and tell a storm-tossed stranger what land this is and who rules here." She answered: "I am no goddess. I am only a Tyrian girl. This is Libya, a land of fierce people. The growing city you see is Carthage, a Tyrian colony ruled by Dido. She fled from Tyre to escape her brother's hatred." Venus then told the long story of how Dido's brother Pygmalion murdered her husband Sichaeus for his gold, and how Sichaeus's ghost appeared to Dido, revealed the crime, and showed her where treasure was hidden. Dido gathered companions, seized ships loaded with gold, and sailed away. A woman led the way. They landed here and bought a stretch of land, as much as could be enclosed by a bull's hide. "But where do you come from? What do you seek on Libyan shores?"

Aeneas sighed deeply, and with sorrow streaming from his eyes, replied: "If you had the patience to listen, the tale of our suffering would take more than a day to tell. We are exiles from ancient Troy, driven by storms across many seas. At last we landed on this Libyan coast. I am Aeneas, a man of duty, carrying my household gods rescued from our enemies. My goal is fruitful Italy, for I am descended from Jupiter himself. I set out from Troy with twenty ships, following fate and my goddess mother's guidance. Now barely seven remain. A stranger in this unknown desert, cast out from Europe and Asia alike, I wander alone."

His mother could bear no more. She interrupted to soothe his grief: "Whoever you are, heaven has not abandoned you. You have been guided to a friendly shore. Take courage and trust the gods. See those twelve swans flying in formation? Just now Jupiter's eagle scattered them, but they have regrouped. Your scattered fleet is likewise safe. Your ships have reached the harbor, or are entering it now. Go forward, follow this path to the city."

As she spoke, she turned. Her neck shone with radiant beauty, and her loosened hair spread divine fragrance all around. Her gown swept the ground, and by her graceful walk she revealed herself as the Queen of Love. Aeneas called after her: "Why do you deceive your own son with disguises? Why not let me embrace you and speak to you face to face?" But though he complained, he obeyed her command. Venus wrapped him and Achates in a cloud of mist, making them invisible. Then she flew up to Paphos, her beloved home, where a hundred altars smoked with incense and offerings of flowers.

Climbing the hill, they looked down and saw the rising city of Carthage. Aeneas marveled at the stately towers, which had recently been nothing but shepherds' huts. He watched the gates, the busy streets, the noisy marketplace. The Tyrians were hard at work. Some extended the city walls. Others built the citadel. Strong men dug foundations or rolled heavy stones along. Some laid out plots for houses and marked them with ditches. Others drafted laws, elected senators, or quarried marble for a theater. They were like bees in early summer, leading their young ones out to labor, storing honey in their cells, relieving the returning foragers of their golden burdens, and driving the lazy drones from the hive. "How fortunate are those whose walls already rise!" Aeneas said. Then he entered the gate, still concealed in cloud, and passed unseen through the busy crowd.

In the center of the city stood a sacred wood. Here, the Tyrians had first dug up a horse's head, an omen of future military glory. Dido had built a magnificent temple to Juno on this spot, rich with gifts and crowned with a golden shrine. Bronze steps led up to a marble threshold, and the doors swung on bronze hinges. What first caught Aeneas's eye revived his courage and calmed his fear. On the temple walls, painted in vivid detail, were scenes from the Trojan War. He recognized Agamemnon, Priam, and fierce Achilles. He stopped and wept. "Even here, my friend, the story of Troy's suffering is known. Even here, human misery finds compassion." He gazed at the scenes: Greeks fleeing, Trojans pursuing, then Achilles driving in his chariot over the slain. He saw the tents of Rhesus, betrayed by their white sails in the night, raided by Diomedes. He saw young Troilus, outmatched by Achilles, dragged by his own horses. He saw the Trojan women processing to Athena's temple, pleading in vain. He saw Achilles dragging Hector's body three times around Troy's walls, and old Priam stretching out his hands to ransom his dead son. He saw himself among the Greek warriors on the battlefield. He recognized dark Memnon with his eastern troops, and Penthesilea, the Amazon queen, leading her warrior women with fierce grace.

While Aeneas stood gazing in wonder at these scenes, the beautiful Dido arrived. With a great retinue of guards and attendants, she ascended the sacred temple. She was like Diana when she leads her band of nymphs, towering above them all. Latona watches with silent pride. Dido moved with equal grace, radiant among her people. She mounted her throne before the shrine and set about the business of governing: hearing petitions, dispensing justice, and dividing labor fairly among her people. Then, from another direction, Aeneas spotted his missing friends: Antheus, Sergestus, brave Cloanthus, and a great crowd of Trojans, all those the storm had scattered to distant shores. Overjoyed but cautious, he watched from his cloud as they approached the queen. Sent as envoys, they entered the temple and spoke.

"O Queen," said Ilioneus, their spokesman, "favored by heaven to found an empire in these lands, we are wretched Trojans, tossed across every sea. We beg your mercy. Do not burn our ships. Do not attack us. We are not raiders or pirates. We came from Hesperia, a western land also called Italy. We were bound there when storms drove us off course and onto these shores. What kind of people deny even the bare beach to shipwrecked strangers? Our king was Aeneas. No juster lord ever drew a sword. If he still lives, we have nothing to fear, and neither will you regret your kindness. We have allies in Sicily too, where King Acestes rules. Let us repair our ships and, if our prince is safe, sail for Italy. But if he is lost, and our young Iulus with him, then at least let us return to Sicily."

The queen lowered her eyes, then spoke briefly: "Trojans, set aside your fears. The harsh circumstances of my own new kingdom force me to guard these shores. But who has not heard of Troy's suffering and the valor of its people? We Tyrians are not so ignorant. Whether you make for Italy or Sicily, I will help you. Your men will be welcomed, your ships repaired. I will provide an escort for your safe passage. Or, if you wish, stay here and share my city. My wealth, my kingdom, and I myself are yours. I only wish your king had come ashore here too. I will send scouts to search every corner of this coast for him."

Aeneas and Achates, hidden in their cloud, could bear the suspense no longer. Achates urged: "What are we waiting for? Your fleet is safe, your friends are here. Only Orontes is missing, swallowed by the sea before our eyes. Everything else matches what your mother foretold." He had scarcely finished when the cloud dissolved around them and daylight poured in.

The Trojan prince stood revealed in the open, radiant and majestic. His mother Venus had touched him with divine beauty. His hair curled with grace, his eyes sparkled, and his face glowed with youthful vigor. He shone like polished ivory or marble set in gold.

"I am the one you seek," he said. "Trojan Aeneas, snatched from the Libyan waves. I stand before your throne, a prince who owes his life to you alone. O gracious queen, you who alone have pitied the remnants of Troy, who welcome the shipwrecked and the destitute, what thanks can wretched fugitives return? If there is justice among gods or men, may heaven reward your goodness. What happy age produced you, what noble parents gave you birth? While rivers flow to the sea and shadows sweep across the hills, your honor and your name will endure forever." He embraced his friends one by one: Ilioneus, Sergestus, Cloanthus, brave Gyas, and all the rest.
Queen Dido stood fixed on his face, struck by his nobility and beauty. "What fate has driven you through such dangers to our shores?" she asked. "Are you truly Aeneas, born of Venus and Anchises?"

"I remember when I was a child," she continued, "Teucer came to Sidon, an exile seeking my father's help. My father Belus was making war on Cyprus then. From Teucer I first heard of Troy and its heroes. He praised the Trojan valor highly, and even claimed Trojan ancestry for himself. Come in, noble guest. I too have known misfortune. Like you, I was an exile until heaven gave me this place of rest. Suffering has taught me to pity those who suffer." She led him to her palace and proclaimed a great feast. She sent provisions to his ships: twenty oxen, a hundred boars, a hundred lambs with their mothers, and jars of wine. Inside the palace, purple hangings covered the walls. Tables were laden with massive silver plate and golden cups, priceless works of art showing the deeds of her ancestors.

Aeneas, unable to bear his son's absence any longer, sent Achates to the ships to bring young Iulus. He also ordered gifts to be brought: a robe of golden tissue, a veil that had once been Helen's, brought from Argos, a gift from her mother Leda. There was also the scepter that Priam's eldest daughter had carried, her jeweled necklace, and her golden crown. Faithful Achates hurried to carry out these orders.

But Venus, anxious about the Tyrians and fearful that Juno's influence over Carthage might turn Dido against her son, devised a new plan. She summoned Cupid. "My son," she said, "your power alone can defy the Thunderer himself. I need your help. You know how Juno persecutes your brother Aeneas. Dido entertains him now, but I fear for the future. Take the form of young Ascanius. When Dido holds you on her lap at the feast, breathe your hidden fire into her heart. Make her love Aeneas so deeply that nothing can change it." Cupid obeyed gladly. He set aside his wings and quiver and took on the perfect likeness of the boy.

Venus carried the real Ascanius away to a gentle sleep in her sacred groves. Cupid, disguised as the boy, followed Achates to the palace bearing the gifts. Dido sat in splendor on a golden couch. Aeneas was at her side. The Trojans and Tyrians reclined around them. Attendants brought water for their hands, bread in heaped baskets, and towels of silk. Fifty handmaids tended the altar fires while a hundred more served the food and wine. The Tyrian guests gazed in wonder at the gifts and even more at the beautiful boy, his glowing cheeks, his bright eyes. They did not know the god in disguise. But Dido, already doomed to love, could not take her eyes off him. The crafty god played around the hero, then climbed into the queen's lap. She embraced him with fierce delight. Cupid, mindful of his mother's command, worked his way into her willing heart. He blotted out the memory of her dead husband Sichaeus and filled her mind entirely with Aeneas.

When hunger was satisfied and the tables cleared, golden bowls brimming with wine were brought out. Lamps hanging from gilded ceilings cast their warm light through the hall. Dido called for the great bowl that Belus and all her ancestors had used, filled it with wine, and spoke: "O Jupiter, god of hospitality, bless this hour for Trojans and Tyrians alike. May this day mark the beginning of a lasting friendship. Bacchus, giver of joy, and gracious Juno, be present." She poured a libation, then sipped from the cup and passed it along. Bitias took it and drained it to the bottom. The cup went round. The poet Iopas sang of the wandering moon, the origins of men and beasts, the causes of rain and fire, and why winter nights are long and summer nights are short. The Tyrians applauded, and the Trojans joined in. The unhappy queen talked late into the night, drinking deep draughts of love. She asked about Priam, about Hector, about Memnon's armor and Diomedes' horses. At last, as fate and her unlucky stars demanded, she said: "Tell me everything, my noble guest. Tell me of the Greek stratagems, how Troy was betrayed, your wanderings and your sorrows. For seven years, through every sea and every coast, you have been tossed by storms."

chapters.title: Book II
paragraphs: Aeneas tells how Troy was taken after a ten-year siege, through the treachery of Sinon and the stratagem of the wooden horse. He describes his resolve not to survive his country's ruin, and the many dangers he faced defending it. At last, warned by Hector's ghost and the appearance of his mother Venus, he agrees to leave the city and carry his household gods to a new land. He carries his father on his shoulders, leads his small son by the hand, and his wife follows behind. When he reaches the meeting point, he finds a great crowd of refugees but discovers his wife is missing. Her ghost appears and tells him the land that fate has chosen for him.

Everyone fell silent and turned their eyes on the prince. From his raised couch, Aeneas began: "Great queen, what you ask me to recall renews the terrible memory of our fate. You ask me to relive an empire torn from its ancient foundations, and every sorrow the Trojans endured. I saw it all, and played my part in it. Not even the hardest of our enemies could hear this story without tears, nor could stern Ulysses himself tell it dry-eyed. The late hour and the setting stars invite us to rest. But since you wish to know of Troy's disastrous end, I will hold back my tears and briefly tell what happened on our last and fatal night."

"The Greeks, worn out after years of fruitless war, built a monstrous wooden horse with Athena's help. They pretended it was an offering for their safe return home. But inside its hollow belly, they hid their best soldiers, packed tight with weapons in the dark. Near Troy lies the island of Tenedos, once wealthy and famous, now just an exposed bay. The Greek fleet hid behind it. We thought they had sailed for home. All Troy threw open its gates. People swarmed out like bees, delighted to see the deserted camp. They pointed out where this chief or that one had camped, where Achilles pitched his tent, where the ships were drawn up, where the battles raged. All eyes turned to the monstrous horse, Athena's gift built to destroy us. Thymoetes urged that it be dragged inside the walls. But Capys and others with sounder judgment wanted to burn it or throw it in the sea, or at least bore into its hollow sides. The crowd was divided. Then Laocoon came running from the fortress and cried out: 'Are you mad? Do you think the Greeks have really gone? Don't you know Ulysses better than that? Either Greek soldiers are hiding inside, or this is a siege engine built to overlook our walls. Something treacherous is at work. Do not trust this horse!' He hurled his spear into its side. It stuck, trembling in the belly, and the hollow insides groaned. If the gods had not blinded us, we would have torn the thing apart and Troy would still be standing. But just then, Trojan shepherds dragged in a Greek captive, bound in chains. He had let himself be caught on purpose, ready to die or deceive. The Trojans crowded around him, mocking and curious. He trembled, looked around with wild eyes, and cried: 'What land, what sea is left for me? I am scorned by my enemies and abandoned by my own people.' His tears moved us to pity. We urged him to speak freely.

"His fear at last dismissed, Sinon began his tale. 'Whatever fate has in store for me, my words will be honest. I am Greek. My name is Sinon. Fortune may have made me wretched, but she cannot make me a liar. You may have heard of Palamedes, whom Ulysses destroyed through false charges because Palamedes opposed the war. When my kinsman Palamedes fell, I was left alone and powerless. I mourned him openly and swore revenge if I ever returned to Greece. That sealed my doom. Ulysses spread rumors against me and plotted my death. He forced the prophet Calchas to name me as a sacrifice. But why go on? If being Greek is enough to condemn me, then strike now. My death would please the sons of Atreus and delight Ulysses.' His broken speech and pretended terror only made us more curious.
"He continued his false tale: 'The Greeks had long wanted to abandon the siege, but storms kept driving them back. They consulted the oracle, which gave a terrible answer.'

"'Greeks, you bought your passage to Troy with a virgin's blood. Your return must be bought with Greek blood,' the oracle declared. Everyone feared being chosen. Ulysses forced Calchas to name the victim. For ten days the old prophet resisted, until at last he gave in and pronounced my name. All were relieved that the storm would fall on one man alone. The dreadful day came. The priests prepared the sacred cakes and ribbons for my hair. But I broke my bonds and fled into the night. I hid in a weedy lake until they sailed away. Now I can never see my homeland again. My children, my old father, will pay for my escape with their lives. By all that is sacred, by the gods above, have pity on a man who has suffered more than he deserves.'

"His false tears moved us to true pity. King Priam ordered his chains removed and spoke kindly to him: 'Forget the Greeks. You are one of us now. But tell me truly: why did they build this enormous horse? Was it for war, or was it a religious offering?' Sinon, full of cunning, raised his freed hands to heaven and cried: 'You eternal fires of heaven, you sacred altars from which I fled, bear witness that I betray the Greeks without guilt! They deserve it. Hear me, king, and keep the faith you have given. All Greek hopes rested on Athena's favor. But when impious Diomedes and lying Ulysses stole her sacred statue from her temple, murdered the sleeping guards, and touched the virgin image with their bloody hands, the tide of fortune turned against the Greeks. Their courage failed and Athena withdrew her aid. Her stolen image, when it touched the ground, rolled its glaring eyes, sweated drops of brine, and leaped three times from the earth, brandishing its lance and shaking its dreadful shield. Calchas declared that the Greeks must sail home and seek Athena's favor again with fresh prayers. They built this horse as an offering to appease her, and made it so huge that it could never pass through your gates. For if you bring it inside, Troy will be safe forever and will one day conquer Greece itself. But if you harm it, Troy will burn.'

"With such lies he won their trusting hearts. What neither Diomedes nor Achilles, what a thousand ships and ten years of siege could not accomplish, false tears and a smooth tongue achieved. They conquered the city with words.

"A greater omen followed, one that sealed our doom. While Laocoon was sacrificing a bull at Neptune's altar, two monstrous serpents came gliding across the sea from Tenedos. Their flaming crests rose above the waves, their bellies seemed to burn the water beneath them. They reached the shore and made straight for Laocoon and his two young sons. They coiled around the boys first, crushing their small bodies. When the father ran to help, the serpents seized him too, wrapping twice around his waist and twice around his throat. Their heads towered above him as he struggled to tear their coils apart. His sacred ribbons dripped with venom. His screams filled the air like the bellowing of a wounded bull that breaks free from the altar. Their work done, the serpents glided to Athena's temple and coiled at her feet, sheltered by her shield. Everyone cried that Laocoon deserved his fate for daring to strike the sacred horse. They voted to breach the walls and drag the horse inside. They fastened wheels to its feet and hauled it with ropes. Boys and girls crowned with garlands sang and danced around it. Four times it stuck at the gate, and four times the clash of hidden weapons rang out. But blind with zeal, we dragged it in and placed the deadly engine within our towers. Cassandra warned us, but by the god's decree, no one believed her prophecy. We decked the temples with festive branches and celebrated what would be our last day. Night fell. The Greek fleet sailed silently back from Tenedos, guided by the flagship's signal fire. Sinon crept to the horse and opened its trapdoor. The hidden warriors slid down ropes into the dark: Thessander, Sthenelus, dire Ulysses, Thoas, Athamas, Pyrrhus, and many more. They killed the sleeping sentries and opened the gates for their comrades.

"It was the dead of night, that hour when sleep heals our weary bodies and troubled minds. The ghost of Hector appeared before me, weeping and disfigured. His feet were swollen from the thongs that had dragged him behind Achilles' chariot. His body was black with dust and gore. He looked nothing like the Hector who had returned in triumph wearing Achilles' armor, or who had hurled fire at the Greek ships. His hair and beard were stiff with blood, and all his wounds streamed fresh. I wept at the sight and cried out: 'O light of Troy, our greatest hope! Where have you been so long? How we have needed you! But what wounds are these? What new disgrace has marred your noble face?'

"The ghost ignored my questions. Groaning from the depths of his chest, he spoke these mournful words: 'Flee, son of the goddess! Escape the flames of this fatal night! The enemy holds the walls. Troy falls from its great height. Enough has been given to Priam and to duty. If mortal hands could have saved this city, mine would have done it. Now Troy entrusts her future to you. Take her gods as companions of your fate. Wander long, and at last you will build great walls for them.' He said this, and brought me the sacred statues and the holy fire of Vesta from their blessed shrines.

"The sounds of war grew louder. Though our palace stood apart among the trees, I could hear the clash of weapons and the screams of the dying. I shook off sleep, climbed to the roof, and looked out. It was like watching a fire driven by wind mow through a standing crop, or a mountain flood sweep away fields, forests, and flocks. The shepherd on his cliff stares in helpless wonder. Now Hector's warning proved true. The palace of Deiphobus blazed high, and his neighbor Ucalegon's house caught fire next. The sea glowed bright with reflected flames. Trumpets blared and war cries echoed. Seized with desperate courage, I grabbed my weapons. I had no plan, but I burned to gather friends and make a stand, or at least to die fighting.

"Pantheus, Apollo's priest, came running to my door, clutching the sacred relics and leading his young grandson by the hand. 'What hope remains, Pantheus? Where can we make a stand?' I asked. He groaned: 'Troy is finished. The fatal day has come. Jupiter has handed our city to the Greeks. The horse has burst open. Armed men pour out. Sinon fans the flames everywhere. Thousands more press through the gates. Every street is blocked. Those who resist are killed. Those who flee are cut down. The gate guards barely hold their ground.'

"Inspired by heaven and desperate courage, I gathered companions: Ripheus, Iphitus, old Dymas, Hypanis, and young Coroebus, who had come to win Cassandra's hand and fight for Troy, heedless of her own prophetic warnings. When I saw them all resolved to die, I said: 'Brave men, your courage is wasted on a doomed cause, but if you are determined to follow me to the end, then come. You can see how things stand. The gods have abandoned their own temples. We fight for a city already in flames. Let us fall, but let us fall among our enemies. The hopeless have nothing left to lose.' My words fed their fury.

"Like hungry wolves driven by need, we plunged through the dark streets. What tongue can tell the slaughter of that night? An ancient imperial city was falling. Bodies filled the streets and the holy temples. Trojan blood ran everywhere, but not only ours. The vanquished sometimes triumphed and the victors fell. Grief and terror filled every corner, and death appeared in a thousand forms. We ran into Androgeos and his band of Greeks, who mistook us for their own. 'Hurry up,' he called. 'The ships are being loaded with plunder and you come late!' Then he realized his mistake. He was like a man who steps on a snake in the brush and recoils in horror. We surrounded them and cut them all down. Flushed with this success, Coroebus had a bold idea: 'Let us put on their armor and carry their shields. Deception can serve where strength fails.' We stripped the dead and disguised ourselves as Greeks. Mixed among the enemy, we killed many more in the dark. Some Greeks fled back to their ships. Others, overcome with terror, climbed back into the hollow horse and hid there.

"But valor is useless when the gods refuse their aid. We saw Cassandra being dragged by her hair from Athena's temple, her tender arms bound, her eyes raised to heaven in helpless prayer. Coroebus could not bear the sight. He charged into the Greek raiders and we followed. But stones rained down on us from the temple roof, thrown by our own Trojans who mistook our borrowed Greek armor for the real thing. Meanwhile the Greeks, furious at seeing their captive rescued, rallied from every side: the sons of Atreus, Ajax, and the whole Thessalian cavalry.

"It was like rival winds tearing a forest apart, churning the sea until sand and mud darken the sky. The troops we had scattered regrouped and surrounded us. They noticed our different speech and saw through our borrowed armor. We were overwhelmed. Coroebus fell first, struck down at Athena's altar by Peneleus. Ripheus fell too, the most just and righteous man in all of Troy, though the gods thought otherwise. Dymas and Hypanis were killed by their own friends who did not recognize them. Not even Pantheus, with his priestly robes and Apollo's sacred bands, was spared. O flames of Troy, bear witness: I did not avoid any sword in that slaughter. I was ready to die and deserved the death I sought. But fate swept me away. Old Iphitus and wounded Pelias and I were carried off by the retreating crowd. New clamors drew us toward Priam's palace, where the fighting was fiercest of all. It was as if no other battle raged in the whole city. The Greeks advanced in tortoise formation, raised ladders against the walls, and clung to pillars and doorposts. The Trojans tore off gilded rooftops, marble pillars, and heavy beams to hurl down on the attackers. The guards below held the gate with grim determination. We rushed in to reinforce them, to relieve the exhausted and avenge the dead.

"A hidden postern door, connected by a long dark gallery, led to the king's private chambers. Hector's wife Andromache had often used this passage to bring little Astyanax to see his grandfather. Through it, we climbed to the tower from which the defenders hurled their futile missiles. From its height, old Priam had often watched the Greek camp and their ships at anchor. We hacked at the tower's beams with swords, wrenched them loose, and pushed whole sections down on the attackers. The crash was louder than thunder. The Greeks below were crushed to pieces, but more kept coming. Before the gate stood Pyrrhus, gleaming in bronze, like a snake that has shed its winter skin and emerges in spring, renewed and glistening in the sun, coiling high with its forked tongue flickering. With him came Periphas, fierce Automedon, and the Scyrian infantry. They hurled firebrands onto the roof while Pyrrhus himself hacked at the doors with his axe. Blow after blow he struck until the bronze hinges gave way and a great breach opened. The inner halls were exposed. Armed soldiers swarmed past shrieking women. The palace filled with cries and lamentation. Pyrrhus drove through everything, unstoppable as a raging flood that bursts its dams and sweeps away cattle and homes. I saw him myself, marching between the sons of Atreus. I saw the queen, the hundred wives, and old Priam at the altar, about to stain it with his own blood. The fifty bridal chambers, those proud tokens of a dynasty's hopes, their gilded pillars hung with spoils, all fell to the conqueror. Wherever fire left a space, Greeks swarmed in and took possession.

"Perhaps you wish to know Priam's fate. When the old king saw his palace invaded and his gates torn down, he strapped on his ancient armor, useless as it was, and buckled on a sword he had not worn in years. His feeble shoulders could barely carry the weight. He was not armed but burdened, creeping toward death. Near the hearth stood an altar beneath an old laurel tree that sheltered the household gods. There Hecuba and her daughters huddled together like doves driven by a storm, clutching the sacred images. When she saw Priam in his armor, she cried: 'What madness has seized you, husband? These times need other help. Even Hector could do nothing now. Come sit with us. This altar will protect us all, or we will die together.' She drew him down beside her. But then young Polites, one of Priam's sons, came running through the halls pursued by Pyrrhus. Wounded and stumbling, he fled through empty corridors with Pyrrhus close behind, thrusting at him again and again. At last, before his parents' eyes, the boy fell and bled out his life. Old Priam, shaking more with anger than with fear, cried out: 'May the gods repay your cruelty! If there is justice in heaven, your punishment will come. You made a father watch his son's murder. Even Achilles, the man you claim as your father, never treated me so. He respected my grief, returned Hector's body, and sent me safely home.'
"The old man hurled his feeble javelin. It barely reached Pyrrhus's shield and fell, clanging uselessly against the bronze.

"Pyrrhus sneered: 'Go carry your complaints to my father in the underworld. Now die.' He dragged the trembling king through his murdered son's blood, twisted his hand in the old man's white hair, and drove his sword through his side. So fell Priam, who once had ruled all Asia and commanded the obedience of nations. His great body lay abandoned on the shore, a headless corpse, a nameless thing.

"Horror seized me then. I thought of my own father Anchises, who was the same age as Priam. I thought of my wife Creusa and my little son Iulus. I looked around and found myself alone. All my companions had deserted me. Some had leaped from the burning walls. Others had given themselves to the flames. Then, by the flickering firelight, I spotted Helen lurking in the porch of Vesta's temple, hiding in the shadows. She feared the Trojans for the ruin she had caused and the Greeks for the husband she had betrayed. Rage burned in me. 'Shall this woman sail home in triumph,' I thought, 'while Troy lies in ashes and Priam lies murdered? Shall she return to Sparta attended by captive servants? Killing a woman brings no glory, but destroying this curse will satisfy my soul and avenge my people.' But as I moved toward her, a brilliant light filled the air. My mother Venus appeared before me, radiant and divine, more glorious than I had ever seen her. She caught my hand and stopped the blow. 'My son, what madness is this? Think of your father, your wife, your child. Greeks surround your house, and only my protection keeps them alive. It is not Helen's beauty or Paris's guilt that destroyed Troy. The gods themselves have done this. Look.' She cleared the mist from my eyes, and I saw Neptune himself shaking Troy's foundations with his trident, Juno standing at the Scaean gate urging the Greeks forward, Athena on the tower with her dreadful shield, and Jupiter arming the enemy gods against us. 'Flee, my son. I will guard your way.' She vanished into the darkness. I looked and saw the monstrous shapes of angry gods. Troy was sinking like a great mountain ash hacked by woodsmen, swaying with each blow until at last it groans and crashes down, spreading ruin across the plain.

"I made my way home through fire and enemies. My father Anchises refused to leave. 'Go, save yourselves,' he said. 'I have lived long enough. I have already seen Troy fall once before, when Hercules sacked it. That was enough for one lifetime. Leave me here to die. The enemy will strip my body soon enough. As for a tomb, let heaven provide. Ever since Jupiter struck me with his lightning for loving Venus, I have dragged out a hated life.' Nothing could move him. My wife, my son, my whole household begged him with tears and cries. 'Will you drag us all down with you?' we pleaded. But he stood firm in his refusal.

"Driven by despair, I strapped on my armor again, resolved to die fighting. 'Father, did you think I could leave you behind? If Troy must be destroyed to the last stone, then let Pyrrhus come. Let me face him with his father's blood still on his sword. Is this why my mother saved me through fire and battle, only to watch my father, my wife, and my son slaughtered together in our own house? Give me back my weapons. Let me die with honor. The Greeks will not see me fall unavenged.' As I headed for the door, Creusa threw herself at my feet, holding up little Iulus. 'If you go to die, take us with you. But if you have any hope left, defend this house first.' While she spoke, a miracle happened. A tongue of flame appeared above Iulus's head, playing harmlessly around his temples. We rushed to put it out, but my father Anchises raised his hands to heaven and cried: 'Almighty Jupiter, if any prayer can move you, confirm this sign!' Barely had he spoken when thunder crashed on our left and a shooting star blazed across the sky, trailing fire over the rooftops and disappearing into the forests of Mount Ida.
"'No more delay,' my father said. 'I yield. I follow wherever heaven leads. Gods of our country, preserve this child. This omen is yours. Troy is in your hands. I am ready to go.'

"The fire was drawing closer, rolling through the streets in waves. 'Father, climb on my shoulders,' I said. 'Whatever happens, we share one fate. Little Iulus, take my hand. Creusa, follow close behind. Servants, meet us at the ruined temple of Ceres outside the walls. There is an old cypress there that has stood for generations. We will gather there.' I covered my shoulders with a lion skin, lifted my father, and took my son's hand. Creusa followed in our footsteps. I who had faced Greek spears and the shock of battle without flinching now trembled at every shadow, fearful not for myself but for those I carried. We had nearly reached the gate when the tramp of marching feet rang out. My father peered through the darkness and cried: 'Run! I see the gleam of shields and swords!' In my panic, I took a wrong turn through winding alleys, seeking the shelter of dark side streets. And there I lost Creusa. Whether she stopped from exhaustion, lost her way, or was struck down by fate, I never knew. I did not realize she was gone until we reached the temple of Ceres and found her missing from among our company.

"I went mad with grief. I cursed every god and man. I left my father, my son, and my country's gods in the care of my companions and plunged back into the burning city in full armor, ready to face any danger. I retraced every step. Every street was filled with horror, and even the silence was terrifying. I went to our house first, hoping she might have returned. Instead, I found it full of Greeks and already in flames. I searched Priam's palace and the citadel. In Juno's temple, Greek guards watched over piles of Trojan treasure: golden bowls from burning altars, purple robes, the sacred tables of the gods. Lines of captive women and children stood in chains. I called Creusa's name through the empty streets, again and again, until at last her ghost appeared before me. She was larger than in life, pale and shimmering. My hair stood on end. She spoke gently: 'Do not give yourself to grief, dear husband. This is the will of the gods. Heaven forbids me to travel with you. Long wanderings lie ahead, hard labors on land and sea. At last you will reach Latium, where the gentle Tiber flows through green meadows. There you will find a kingdom and a royal bride. Do not weep for me. I will never be a slave to some proud Greek mistress. The great Mother of the gods keeps me here. Farewell, and love the son we share.' I tried to embrace her, three times reaching out, but three times her shade slipped through my arms like a breath of wind or an empty dream.

"When at last I returned to my companions, I was amazed to find their numbers had swollen. A wretched crowd of exiles, men and women, young and old, had gathered with their possessions, ready to follow me over the sea to whatever land I chose. The morning star was rising over Mount Ida, and the Greeks held the gates. There was no more hope of rescue. I gave in to fate, lifted my father on my shoulders, and led the way toward the mountains.

chapters.title: Book III
paragraphs: Aeneas continues his tale. He describes the fleet he built and his first voyage to Thrace. From there he sails to Delos and asks the oracle where the gods want him to settle. Misunderstanding the oracle, he settles in Crete. His household gods appear in a dream and reveal the true meaning. He follows their guidance and sets course for Italy. He is blown to many shores and meets with surprising adventures, until at last he lands on Sicily, where his father Anchises dies. It was from Sicily that he was sailing when the tempest struck and cast him on the Carthaginian coast.

"When heaven overthrew the Trojan state and proud Priam's throne fell to the flames, when ruined Troy became the Greeks' prize, we gathered at the foot of Mount Ida. Warned by celestial omens, we cut timber from the sacred groves and built a fleet. We did not yet know where the gods meant us to settle. Friends flocked to join us daily. In early spring, my father Anchises gave the order to sail. With tears and heavy sighs, I left my native shore and the empty fields where Troy once stood. My father, my son, our household gods great and small, all put to sea together."

"Across from our coast lay Thrace, once a land allied with Troy. I landed there and began to build a city, naming it Aenos after myself. I offered sacrifices to Venus and Jupiter. But when I went to cut branches from the myrtle bushes on a nearby hill to shade our altars, a dreadful thing happened. The first plant I pulled dripped black blood from its torn roots. I tried a second, and it bled the same. Shaking with horror, I prayed to the wood nymphs and the god of war, then pulled a third time with all my strength. A groan rose from deep in the earth, and a voice cried out: 'Why do you tear my buried body, Aeneas? Spare me! I am Polydore, your countryman. The spears that killed me have taken root and grown into these bloody trees. Flee this cursed shore!'"

"I was horrified. Priam had sent young Polydore here when Troy was losing the war, loaded with gold and entrusted to the king of Thrace. But when Troy fell, the faithless king betrayed his guest, murdered the boy for his treasure, and joined the winning side. O cursed hunger for gold, what crimes will men not commit? I called my father and the Trojan elders together and told them what had happened. They all agreed: we must leave this polluted land. But first we held funeral rites for Polydore. The women walked in mourning procession around the tomb, crowned with dark cypress, and we poured offerings of warm milk and blood, calling his spirit three times to rest."
"When the storms abated and gentle southern winds called us to sea, we launched our ships with a favorable breeze and left the cities and shores of Thrace behind."

"We came to an island in the Aegean, sacred to Neptune and Doris. It had once floated free on the waves until Apollo anchored it to the earth. We landed there, grateful for rest, and worshipped at the Sun-god's temple and town."

"Anius, the priest-king of Delos, recognized my father as an old friend and welcomed us to his palace. I went to Apollo's temple and prayed: 'Give us a home, god of Thymbra. We are the weary remnants of Troy. Show us where to go, whom to follow. Speak clearly.' The moment I finished, the ground shook, the laurels trembled, and the whole hill quaked. From the depths of the shrine, a voice boomed: 'Brave Trojans, seek the motherland from which your ancestors first came. That ancient soil will embrace you again. The house of Aeneas will rule the world, and your children's children will wear the crown.' A great shout of joy went up."

"My father, searching his memory, said: 'Listen, princes. The island of Crete, sacred to Jupiter, lies in the middle of the sea with a hundred cities. Our ancestor Teucer came from there before he settled at Troy. Crete must be the motherland Apollo means. It is not far. If Jupiter favors us, we will reach it in three days.' He sacrificed a bull to Neptune and another to Apollo, a white ewe for fair winds and a black one for storms. Word had reached us that Idomeneus, king of Crete, had been driven out, leaving the island free for newcomers."

"We sailed from Delos, passing Naxos with its famous vineyards, green Donysa, Paros with its white marble quarries, and the scattered Cyclades islands. The sailors shouted 'Crete! Crete!' and bent to their oars. We reached the Cretan coast and I founded a city called Pergamea. I assigned homes and fields and gave laws to my people. But a terrible plague struck. The crops withered, the trees died, and a killing pestilence wasted our bodies. My father urged me to sail back to Delos and consult Apollo's oracle again."

"That night, my household gods appeared to me in a vision, radiant in moonlight. They stood at my bedside and spoke: 'Apollo would tell you the same thing if you went back to Delos, so he sends us instead. We followed you from burning Troy. We have crossed the swelling sea with you. We will raise your future children to the stars and give your city an empire. But you must seek another home. This is not the land Apollo meant. There is a place the Greeks call Hesperia, an ancient land, mighty in arms and rich in soil. Its people are called Italians after their king Italus, but some call it Ausonia. That is our true destination. Dardanus, founder of Troy, came from there. Old Iasius too. Rise and tell your aged father: seek Italy, not Crete. Jupiter forbids you Crete.'"

"I was astonished. These were no dreams but waking visions. I saw their faces clearly, the sacred ribbons in their hair, and I broke out in a cold sweat. I leaped up, raised my hands to heaven, and poured a pure offering on the hearth-fire. Then I went to my father and told him everything. He recognized at once that our ancestors had two branches and that he had confused the homelands. 'Now I remember,' he said. 'Cassandra often prophesied this fate for us, calling us to Italy and Hesperia. But who would have believed the Trojans would ever sail so far? Let us obey Apollo.' We gladly made ready to leave."

"We set sail again, leaving a few behind in the abandoned city. Out on the open sea, a violent storm struck. For three days, black clouds hid the sky and thick night blotted out the stars. On the fourth day, the storm broke and we saw the coast of the Strophades islands. There we landed, and finding herds of cattle and goats grazing untended, we slaughtered some and prepared a feast, thanking the gods."

"But the Harpies descended on us. These foul creatures, with women's faces and vulture bodies, snatched at our food with their filthy claws, fouling everything they touched. We moved to a sheltered spot and tried again, but the Harpies returned. I ordered my men to take up arms and fight. They hid in the grass and, when the Harpies came, we charged. But our swords could not pierce their hides. They flew off shrieking, leaving only one behind. Celaeno, their leader, perched on a rock and pronounced a dreadful prophecy: 'You Trojans slaughter our cattle and make war on us? Hear me then. You will reach Italy, but you will not build your city walls until hunger drives you to eat your very tables.' Terrified, we prayed to the gods for mercy and sailed away."

"We sailed on past Ithaca, cursing the homeland of Ulysses. We stopped at Actium, where we held games and I hung a shield on the temple door as a memorial. When the sailing season returned, we put to sea again."

"Wonderful news reached us: Helenus, Priam's son, now ruled in this Greek land. After Troy's fall, he had married Andromache, Hector's widow, and built a little Troy of his own. We sailed to Chaonia and climbed to the city of Buthrotus. There I found Andromache pouring offerings at an empty tomb she had raised for Hector, beside a stream she had named after the Simois."

"When she saw me, she trembled and nearly fainted. 'Are you real?' she whispered. 'Are you truly Aeneas, son of the goddess? Or if you are a ghost, where is Hector?' She burst into tears. I was so moved I could barely answer. 'I am alive,' I said. 'I have survived every danger. What fate has come to you since Troy fell? Does Pyrrhus still claim you as his prize?'"

"'Happy Polyxena,' she said through her tears, 'who was killed at Achilles' tomb and never had to endure captivity. I was dragged from burning Troy as a slave, bore Pyrrhus a son, and suffered every humiliation. When Pyrrhus married Hermione and cast me aside, Helenus received me. But Orestes, mad with rage, murdered Pyrrhus at his own altar. Part of the kingdom passed to Helenus, who named these fields the Chaonian land. He built this little Troy, this miniature citadel, this stream he calls the Xanthus. But what of you? What winds have brought you here? Does little Ascanius still live? Does he still mourn his lost mother Creusa?'"

"Helenus himself then came down to greet us with a great retinue. He recognized his old friends and led us to his city. I saw a miniature Troy: a small citadel named Pergamus, a dry stream called the Xanthus, and a gate that echoed the Scaean gate. My Trojans wandered in wonder through these familiar-looking streets. Helenus feasted us in his palace for days."

"At last I asked him to prophesy our future. Helenus, filled with Apollo's spirit, sacrificed to the gods and led me to his shrine. There, possessed by divine power, he spoke: 'Son of the goddess, the fates conspire for your good and Jupiter himself protects you. I will explain a few things to help you cross the seas safely. The rest the fates conceal from me, and Juno forbids me to speak of them. First: that Italian shore that seems so near is actually far away. You must sail around Sicily, past Circe's island, and even visit the underworld before your city rises. Watch for this sign: when you find a white sow with thirty white piglets on a riverbank, there is the place for your city and the end of your labors. Do not let the prophecy about eating your tables frighten you. Apollo will provide, and fate will find a way. Avoid the coast facing Epirus, for Greeks hold those shores. Stay clear of Idomeneus's territory and the Salentine fields. When you sacrifice on the shore, veil your head with a purple cloth so no hostile face can disturb the rite. Pass this custom down to your descendants.'"

"'When you reach the straits of Sicily,' Helenus continued, 'keep to the left and give the right shore a wide berth. Long ago, Italy and Sicily were one, until an earthquake split them apart and the sea rushed in. Scylla hides on the right, and Charybdis churns on the left, sucking ships down into her whirlpool three times a day and then spitting the water toward the sky. Scylla lurks in a cave with a human face and a maiden's breast, but below the waist she is a mass of sea-wolves and dolphin tails. Better to take the long way around Cape Pachynus than to glimpse Scylla in her rocky den.'"

"'Above all,' he urged, 'worship Juno. Pray to her. Appease her pride with gifts and humble offerings. Only then will you safely reach Italy. When you arrive, go to Cumae. There you will find the Sibyl, a mad prophetess who sits in a dark cave and writes the fates on leaves. She arranges them in order at the cave's mouth, but if a breeze scatters them, she never bothers to collect them. Many seekers leave cursing, their fortunes lost to the wind.'"

"'Go to the Sibyl,' he said. 'Beg her to speak your fate aloud rather than write it on her leaves. She will show you the Italian peoples, the wars to come, and how to face or avoid each trial. Do not grudge the delay, even if your companions urge you to sail. This is what heaven allows me to tell. Go now in peace, and raise the Trojan name to the stars.'"

"Helenus loaded us with gifts: gold, ivory, Dodonean cauldrons, and silver for every ship. He gave me a coat of mail with triple chains of gold, a fine helmet with a plumed crest that once belonged to Pyrrhus. He supplied my father with horses, captains, extra rowers, and arms. My father ordered the sails raised, not wanting to miss the favorable winds."

"Helenus embraced my father with parting words: 'Happy old man, honored by Venus's love and twice saved when Troy fell. Behold, the Italian coast you long for lies across the water. But the shore directly ahead is forbidden to you. The part Apollo means lies farther south. Go with heaven's blessing, and do not let an old friend's useless words delay you when the southern wind calls.'"

"Andromache too brought gifts for Ascanius: robes embroidered with gold, a Phrygian cloak. 'Take these keepsakes, child,' she said, weeping. 'They are the last gifts that Hector's wife can give. You remind me so much of my lost Astyanax. He would have been your age.' I wept as I took my leave."

"With tears I said farewell. 'Your fortunes are already made,' I told them. 'You have found your rest. We must keep searching, sea after sea. You have your own Troy, your own Simois. I pray that if I ever reach the Tiber and build my promised city, our kindred peoples will stay friends forever, united by our shared Trojan blood. May what we begin today endure for all generations.'"

"We sailed close to the cliffs of Ceraunia, the nearest point to Italy. As night fell, we landed on the shore. The sailors took watch in turns while the rest slept on the sand. At midnight, Palinurus the helmsman rose to study the sky. He watched the Pleiades, the Hyades, both Bears, and Orion. Seeing nothing to threaten us, he gave the signal. We broke camp and spread our sails."

"With the dawn, we saw the hills of Italy rising from the mist. 'Italy!' Achates shouted first, and the whole crew took up the cry. My father crowned a cup with wine and prayed to the gods of land and sea for fair winds and safe passage. The breeze freshened and the harbor drew near. We saw Athena's temple on a hilltop. We furled our sails and turned toward shore. The bay curved inward like a bow, shielded by towering rocks. On the beach, four white horses grazed in a meadow. 'War!' my father cried. 'Horses mean war. But horses can also be tamed to the yoke. There may be peace.' We prayed at Athena's temple, veiling our heads as Helenus had instructed, and offered sacrifice to Juno. Then we sailed on without delay."

"Past Tarentum we sailed, past Lacinian Juno's temple, past the towers of Caulon and the shipwreck coast of Scylaceum. Then smoking Etna rose before us, and we heard Charybdis roaring. 'Those are the rocks the prophet warned us of!' cried Anchises. 'Bear off to sea!' Palinurus swung hard to port and every ship followed. We rode the mountainous waves up and down, and three times our keels struck bottom. The wind died with the sun and we drifted, exhausted, to the Cyclops' coast at the foot of thundering Etna. That night was terrible. Etna belched fire and molten rock into the sky. Underground, trapped Enceladus groaned and shifted, shaking the whole island. We huddled in the woods, hearing horrible sounds in the darkness but seeing nothing, for clouds smothered the stars and the moon."

"At dawn, a wretched figure stumbled from the forest toward us: filthy, starving, his clothes held together with thorns. He fell to his knees and begged: 'By heaven and the air we breathe, take me away from here! I am Greek, I admit it. I fought against Troy. Throw me in the sea if you must, but do not leave me on this island.' He clasped my knees, weeping. We calmed him. He was Achaemenides, one of Ulysses's men, left behind when they fled the Cyclops' cave. He told us of the horror: the giant's cave, dark and huge, its floor covered with mangled limbs and blood. He described how Polyphemus seized two Greeks in his enormous hand, dashed them on the rocks, and devoured them, crunching their bones while blood ran across the floor."

"'But Ulysses got his revenge. When the giant lay sleeping, drunk on human blood, we prayed, drew lots, and surrounded him. Together we drove a burning stake into his single enormous eye. The stroke went home and the pupil burst. But hear me: flee now! A hundred Cyclopes like him roam this island, penning their sheep in caves and stalking the mountains. For three months I have hidden in the woods, living on roots and berries, watching the giants from afar, trembling at the sound of their footsteps and their thundering voices. When I saw your ships, I ran to you. Whatever death you give me is better than this.'"

"Even as he spoke, we saw the giant shepherd Polyphemus himself, groping his way down to the familiar shore. He was monstrous and deformed, a walking mountain. His pine-tree staff guided his blind steps. His shaggy sheep trailed behind him, his only comfort. When he waded into the sea and washed the oozing blood from his ruined eye socket, he gnashed his teeth and groaned. He strode deeper, but even the tallest waves barely reached his waist."

"We seized the Greek, hauled him aboard, and rowed for our lives in silent terror. Polyphemus heard the splash of our oars and turned toward the sound, but we were already out of reach. He roared so loud that the sea trembled, the land shook, and Etna echoed. From every mountain and cave, the other Cyclopes came rushing to the shore. We saw them standing there, a grim council of one-eyed giants, tall as oaks, their heads wreathed in cloud. We fled with every oar and sail, hugging the wind. Remembering Helenus's warning, we avoided both Scylla and Charybdis by tacking to port. A north wind from Cape Pelorus drove us south. We passed the rocky mouth of swift Pantagias, the bay of Megara, and low-lying Thapsus, retracing the landmarks Achaemenides pointed out."

"We sailed past the island of Ortygia, where the river Alpheus is said to run underground from Greece to mingle with the fountain Arethusa. We worshipped Diana as Helenus had instructed. Past the quiet waters of Helorus, past Pachynus with its jutting cape, past Camarina and its undrained marsh, past Gela and great Agrigentum, once famous for its horses. We rounded Selinus and the palm groves, threaded the dangerous shallows off Cape Lilybaeum, and at last reached the port of Drepanum. There, after all my labors, after every storm and every coast, I lost my dear father Anchises. He was the comfort of my cares and the companion of all my suffering, saved through a thousand dangers only to die in peace. Not even the prophet Helenus or the Harpy Celaeno had warned me of this, the greatest sorrow of all. Some kind god carried us from that mournful shore to your blessed coast."
With these words, the royal guest ended his tale to the listening queen. He fell silent at last and retired to rest.

chapters.title: Book IV
paragraphs: Dido confides her passion for Aeneas to her sister Anna, and considers marrying him. She organizes a hunting party for his entertainment. Juno, with Venus's consent, raises a storm that separates the hunters and drives Aeneas and Dido into the same cave, where their union takes place. Jupiter sends Mercury to warn Aeneas to leave Carthage. Aeneas prepares secretly to depart. When Dido discovers his plan, she tries everything to stop him: her own pleas, her sister's, and every passion a rejected lover can feel. When nothing works, she plans her own death, with which this book ends.

But anxious cares had already seized the queen. She nursed an unseen flame in her veins. The hero's courage, his deeds, his noble birth filled her thoughts and fanned the secret fire. His words and his face were imprinted on her heart. When purple dawn chased away the shadows and restored the day, she sought her sister Anna and poured out her troubled thoughts.

"Dearest Anna, what strange dreams torment me! What visions of this Trojan guest disturb my rest! His worth, his bearing, his noble air proclaim him born of gods. I can see he has suffered greatly. How bravely he fought for falling Troy! If I had not sworn after Sichaeus's murder never to submit to marriage again, this one man alone could have shaken my resolve. I confess it, Anna: something stirs in me that feels terribly like my old passion. But let the earth swallow me first, or lightning strike me down, before I break the vow I made to my dead husband. The man who held my love shall keep it in the grave."

She wept. Anna answered: "Sister, dearer to me than life itself, will you waste your youth in solitary grief? Do you think ashes and ghosts in the tomb care about your tears? I grant that mourning suited you at first. You were right to refuse those Libyan and Tyrian suitors. But think! This small kingdom is hemmed in by fierce enemies on every side. Will you also fight against a love that pleases you? Think what a powerful ally these Trojans would make. With such a union, how high your empire could rise! Ask the gods' blessing, make sacrifices, find excuses to keep the Trojans here until winter passes and their broken fleet is repaired."

These words broke down Dido's defenses and added fuel to her flame. She went to every altar, sacrificing choice animals and studying the entrails for signs. She stood before Juno's altar pouring wine between the horns of a white heifer. But what good are prayers and sacrifices for a heart already ablaze? A gentle fire consumed her from within.

Sick with desire, Dido wandered through the city like a wounded deer hit by a shepherd's careless arrow. The shaft stuck in her side, and no amount of running could shake it free. She led Aeneas through the city, showed him her rising towers, and tried to speak her love but always lost her words. When evening came, she begged him to tell his story again, and hung on every word. When at last they parted, she lingered on the couch where he had sat, hearing and seeing him still in his absence.
She sat alone after everyone had gone, clutching young Ascanius to her breast, trying to find the father's image in the child, hoping to deceive her unspoken love.

Meanwhile, the rising towers stood idle. The young men abandoned their training. The harbor walls, the fortifications, the defenses of the city all lay unfinished, reaching toward a sky they would never touch.

Juno saw Dido chained by love and senseless to shame. She approached Venus with smooth words: "What a glorious victory for you and your son! Two gods have conquered one helpless woman. I know you suspect my city. But let us end this quarrel. Let your Trojan and my Tyrian be joined. Dido shall be yours, and Aeneas mine. One kingdom, one united line." Venus saw through the scheme at once. Juno wanted to divert the future empire from Italy to Libya. But she played along: "Who would be fool enough to refuse such an alliance? But I wonder whether Jupiter approves. You are his wife. Sound his will. I will follow your lead."

"Leave Jupiter to me," said Juno. "Now hear my plan. Tomorrow, when the queen and Aeneas go hunting, I will pour down a storm of hail and thunder. The rest of the party will scatter. Aeneas and Dido will take shelter in the same cave. I will be there to bless the union." Venus smiled and said nothing, seeing through the disguised plot.

The rosy morning came. The hunters gathered at the gates with nets, spears, and swift horses. Dido appeared last, dressed magnificently in a gold-fringed cloak, her hair bound in a golden circlet. She rode a splendid horse that pawed the ground and champed a golden bit. Young Ascanius rode with high spirits among the Trojan youth. But shining above them all was Aeneas himself, like Apollo leaving his winter palace at Xanthus to return to Delos, his golden hair wreathed with laurel.

They reached the mountain heights and flushed the wild game from its hiding places. Goats bounded among the crags. Stags raced across the dusty plain. Young Ascanius galloped among them, wishing for a boar or lion instead of these timid creatures.

Then the storm broke. Clouds gathered, lightning flashed, thunder rolled, and Juno poured down a deluge of hail and rain. The hunting party scattered in every direction, seeking shelter in cottages and caves. Aeneas and the queen, guided by love or fate, found themselves alone in the same cave. The earth trembled. Lightning flashed. Nymphs howled on the mountaintops. From that ill-fated hour sprang discord and death and all the suffering that followed.
The queen no longer tried to hide her love. She called it marriage, using that respectable name to veil her shame.

Rumor spread through the Libyan cities. Rumor, that vast and terrible creature, swift and growing. With countless eyes, tongues, and ears, she flies through the world by day and haunts the rooftops by night. She whispers truth and lies alike. She filled the people's ears with Dido's name: how the queen had taken a wandering foreigner into her bed, how both of them wasted the winter in luxury, forgetful of their duties.

Rumor's chief delight was to spread stories that caused terror. She filled the people's ears with Dido's name, saying the queen had lost all sense of honor and shame. A wandering stranger now shared her throne and her bed. They wasted whole days in pleasure and long winter nights in luxury, forgetting royal duty, abandoned to desire.
Rumor carried the story to King Iarbas, a Libyan lord who had once courted Dido and been rejected. He was the son of Jupiter Ammon and had built a hundred temples to his divine father.

Burning with rage, Iarbas knelt at his altar and prayed: "Great Jupiter, do you see this? Or do we fear your thunder for nothing? A homeless woman builds a tiny town on the land I gave her, and then she takes this perfumed Trojan to her bed instead of me? And you do nothing?"

Jupiter heard. He looked down on Carthage and saw the guilty pair lost in pleasure, forgetful of their destinies. He summoned Mercury and gave him stern orders: "Fly to Carthage. Find the Trojan prince wasting his days in shameful leisure. Tell him this is not what his mother Venus twice saved his life for. He was destined to rule a warrior race in Italy and establish a line that would conquer the world. If his own glory cannot move him, let him think of his son Ascanius, who is being cheated of his rightful inheritance. Tell him to leave Carthage at once."

Mercury fastened his golden-winged sandals and flew. He passed over the summit of Atlas, that giant who bears the sky on his shoulders. He dove toward the sea and skimmed across the waves like a fishing bird. When he reached Libya, he found Aeneas supervising the construction of new buildings, wearing a purple cloak embroidered with gold, a gift from Dido, with a jeweled sword hanging idly at his side.

Mercury appeared in his true divine form and said: "Are you building towers for Carthage now, slave to a woman? The almighty ruler of heaven sends you this message: What are you doing in Libya? If your own glory means nothing to you, think of your son. He is owed the throne of Italy and the imperial name of Rome." Having spoken, the god vanished into thin air.

Aeneas was struck dumb with terror. His hair stood on end. He longed to obey immediately and leave this enchanting land. But what could he say to the queen? How could he begin?
