He turned the problem over in his anxious mind and finally decided to prepare the fleet in secret. He would find the right moment and the right words to tell Dido.

But a jealous woman's eyes are sharp. Dido sensed the plan before it was announced. She raged through the city like a wild Bacchant. At last she confronted him: "Did you think you could sneak away without my knowing? Does my love mean nothing? Have you no pity? Even in winter you dare the open sea? If Troy still stood, would you risk these waters? Am I the enemy you flee? By our love, by whatever vows we shared, if I ever pleased you in any way, I beg you: do not go! For your sake I have earned the hatred of my own people. I have lost my honor and my reputation. To whom do you leave me? If only you had given me a child, a little Aeneas who might remind me of his father, I would not feel so utterly abandoned."

Aeneas stood unmoved. Jupiter's command kept his eyes steady, though his heart was breaking. At last he spoke: "Queen, I can never deny your countless kindnesses, nor will I ever forget you. But hear me: I never intended a secret flight, and I never claimed the rights of a husband. If fate allowed me to choose my own life, I would have rebuilt Troy. But Apollo's oracle, my father's ghost, and now a messenger from Jupiter himself all command me to seek Italy. That is my fated home. You, a Tyrian, have built your city on foreign soil. Why should I not be allowed to seek mine? Do not make this harder with your tears. I leave not by my own will. I am called by fate."

She looked at him with blazing eyes, surveying him from head to foot. "Liar! No goddess bore you. You were hewn from rock, suckled by tigers. Did you flinch when I wept? Did you shed one tear? Juno sees this injustice, but no thunder falls. Nowhere is faith safe. I took in this castaway, shared my throne, saved his fleet. Now he claims gods and oracles order him to leave. As if the gods care about him! Go then, seek your Italy through the storms. I pray you will be wrecked on the rocks, calling Dido's name. My ghost will haunt you. I will hear of your punishment, even in the underworld."
She broke off and stumbled away. Her maids caught her fainting and carried her to her ivory bed.

But Aeneas, though he grieved and longed to comfort her, obeyed Jupiter's will. He turned to his fleet. His men swarmed like ants stripping a harvest, streaming from the city to the shore, carrying supplies, dragging oars, caulking the hulls.

Dido watched from her tower. She saw the beach black with men, heard the shouts of the sailors. "O mighty Love," she cried, "what you force on mortals!" She sent Anna to beg one last time: not for the marriage back, only for a short delay, time to learn how to bear the coming grief. But Aeneas would not be moved. He stood like a great oak battered by winds from every direction. The trunk shakes, the leaves fly, but the deep roots hold firm.
Like that oak, Aeneas endured the storm of her pleas. His heart was racked with pity. But his purpose held.

Dido, seeing no hope, began to long for death. Dark omens appeared. The wine she poured on the altar turned to blood. She heard her dead husband's voice calling from his tomb. Owls shrieked on the rooftops in the dead of night. In her dreams, Aeneas rejected her coldly. She wandered through deserted wastelands, seeking her people and finding no one.

She made her plan, hiding death behind a calm face. She told Anna: "I have found a way to bring him back or cure my love. A sorceress from the land of Atlas can bind or unbind the chains of love. Build a pyre in the courtyard. Hang on it the Trojan's clothes, his weapons, and everything he left behind. Place the bed where I lay with him underneath. The priestess says burning these relics will purge my heart."

Anna, suspecting nothing, obeyed. They built the pyre of split oak and pine, hung with garlands of cypress and yew. Dido laid out the Trojan's sword, his robes, and placed his image on the bed she knew too well.

The priestess came with her hair unbound. She invoked Hecate, Night, Erebus, and Chaos. She sprinkled water said to come from the lake of Avernus. She mixed dark herbs and cut the love-charm from a newborn foal's forehead. Dido stood beside her, one foot bare, her gown loosened, summoning heaven and every power that watches over betrayed love.
Night came, deep and still. The sea was calm, the stars silent, the woods and fields asleep. Every creature rested except Dido. Sleep fled her eyes. Rage, despair, and love warred in her heart.

She lay awake, turning over impossible choices. Should she humble herself to Iarbas? Follow the Trojan fleet? Neither was bearable. The thought of trusting herself to a people she had once scorned. The memory of Sichaeus, whom she had betrayed. She resolved at last: death was the only escape. On his ship, Aeneas slept more easily, his mind made up.

Mercury appeared again in his dreams: "Are you sleeping? Can you not see the danger? A woman scorned is planning something terrible. Flee now, while you can. The sea will be covered with her ships and fire if you delay until dawn. Woman is a changeable, dangerous thing."

Aeneas started awake in terror. He roused his men at once: "To the oars! Cut the cables! A god commands us to flee!" He drew his sword and slashed the mooring ropes. His men scrambled aboard in the darkness, and the fleet shot out to sea.

Dawn spread its saffron light across the sky. From her tower, Dido saw the empty harbor and the distant sails. She struck her breast and tore her hair. "He is gone! And I did not arm my ships to follow? Burn his fleet? Kill his son and serve the child's flesh at his father's table? But the outcome would have been uncertain. What did I have to fear? I was already dying. O Sun, O Juno, O Hecate, O Furies, hear my final prayer! If that traitor must reach Italy, as fate demands, then let him face war. Let him be driven from his home, separated from his son. Let him beg for help from strangers and see his friends slaughtered before his eyes. When at last he buys peace on humiliating terms, let him not enjoy it long. Let him fall before his time and lie unburied on the sand. And you, my Tyrians, swear eternal hatred against his people. Let there be no peace between our races, ever. Rise, some avenger, from my ashes, to harry the Trojan settlers with fire and sword, now and for all time to come!"
She sent old Barce, her nurse, to fetch Anna with the pretense of a final sacrifice. Then she climbed the pyre.
Her face was ghastly pale, her rolling eyes red with fury. She shook with the enormity of what she intended.

She mounted the great pile. She unsheathed the Trojan sword, never meant for such a purpose. She looked at the robes, the familiar bed. She paused, weeping, and spoke her last words: "Dear relics of my love, receive a soul freed from its anguish. I have lived my life and run my destined course. I go as a great queen to the shades below. I built a glorious city. I avenged my husband. I punished my brother. What more could fortune have given me, if only the Trojan ships had never touched my shore?" She kissed the couch. "Must I die unavenged? Then let me die. Let the cruel Trojan see these flames from the sea. Let this omen of death follow him on his way."
She spoke, and fell upon the sword. Her attendants screamed. The rumor spread like wildfire through the horrified city, as if Carthage or ancient Tyre itself had been set ablaze.

Anna heard and came running, beating her breast, tearing her hair. "Was this your plan all along? The pyre, the altars, were they meant to deceive me? You leave me alone, destroyed." She climbed the pile and cradled her dying sister, trying to staunch the blood. Three times Dido tried to raise her head. Three times she fell back. Her wandering eyes searched for the light, and finding it, she groaned and turned away.

Juno, pitying Dido's lingering death, sent Iris down from heaven to release her struggling soul. Because Dido had not died by heaven's decree or by her own just desert, but by the madness of love, Proserpine had not yet cut the lock of hair that would free her spirit. Iris descended on her rainbow wings, stood above the dying queen, and said: "By Juno's command, I set you free from your body." She cut the golden hair. At once, the warmth left Dido's limbs. Her life dissolved into the air.

chapters.title: Book V
paragraphs: Sailing from Africa, Aeneas is driven by a storm to Sicily, where his friend Acestes welcomes him. He holds funeral games in honor of his father Anchises. During the festivities, Juno sends Iris to persuade the Trojan women to burn the ships. Four vessels are destroyed before Jupiter sends a miraculous rainstorm to save the rest. Following wise counsel and a vision of his father's ghost, Aeneas founds a city for those unfit or unwilling to continue, then sails for Italy. Venus wins from Neptune a promise of safe passage for the fleet, though one man must be lost. The pilot Palinurus, overcome by the god of Sleep, falls into the sea.

Meanwhile, the Trojan fleet cut through the waves, holding a steady course from Carthage. Looking back, Aeneas saw flames mounting from the Punic shore. He did not know the cause, but the fierce passions of a scorned woman and Dido's desperate nature filled his heart with dark foreboding. Soon the fires faded and only the empty sea remained. But a black cloud gathered overhead, and Palinurus the pilot cried: "A storm is coming! Reef the sails and bend to the oars!" Then he turned to Aeneas: "My lord, not even if Jupiter himself promised Italy could we force a way through this tempest. The wind has shifted against us. But Sicily is near, and we can reach it with hard rowing." Aeneas agreed. "Nothing would please me more than that sacred shore where my father's bones lie and where Acestes rules." They turned before the wind and soon reached the Sicilian port. Acestes, watching from a hilltop, saw the fleet approaching and ran down to greet them, dressed in a rough bearskin, carrying two javelins. Born of Trojan blood and a Sicilian river-god, he welcomed his returning friends with country feasts and generous hospitality.

The next morning, Aeneas gathered his people and spoke from a hill: "My noble Trojans, a full year has passed since we buried my father's ashes on this island. The anniversary of that sacred, sorrowful day has come around. I would honor it with annual games and offerings, even if I were stranded on hostile shores. But since heaven itself has driven us to this friendly coast where Anchises rests, let us celebrate his memory with joy and pray for fair winds. King Acestes has generously provided two steers for every ship. If the ninth day dawns clear, we will hold a boat race, a footrace, boxing, archery, and a cavalry display. Come, everyone, and crown your temples with garlands." He wreathed his own brow with myrtle, and the elders and young Ascanius followed his example.

At the tomb, Aeneas poured two bowls of wine, two of milk, and two of sacred blood, scattering roses over the earth. He spoke to his father's shade: "Hail, dear father, hail, sacred ashes. The gods did not permit you to reach Italy with me, nor to see the Tiber, whatever river that may be." As he spoke, a great speckled serpent glided from the tomb, its massive body coiled in seven loops, its scales gleaming blue and gold. It wound peacefully between the altars, tasted the offerings, then slid back into the earth. Aeneas could not tell if this was his father's guardian spirit or the genius of the place. He renewed his sacrifices with greater zeal: five sheep, five swine, five black bulls, and fresh wine. His companions came in a long procession, adding their own offerings of oxen and entrails roasted over the flames.

The day of the games arrived. The surrounding peoples came to watch and compete. Prizes were displayed in the center: laurel crowns, palm branches, weapons, tripods, gold and silver ingots, and purple robes. Four matched galleys entered the watery lists. The swift Dolphin carried Mnestheus. Gyas commanded the towering Chimaera, a floating city. Sergestus led in the great Centaur. Cloanthus stood on the sea-green Scylla.

Far out in the sea stood a rock, submerged in storms but visible in calm weather. Aeneas set an oak branch on its summit as the turning mark. The crews took their places. Lots were drawn. The sailors oiled their shoulders and gripped their oars, hearts pounding with hope and fear. At the trumpet's blast, they shot forward. The shouts of the crowd echoed from hill to hill. Their oars churned the water to foam, cutting furrows as deep as any chariot race.

Gyas led at first, with Cloanthus close behind, better manned but slowed by his heavy ship. The Centaur and Dolphin fought for third. Nearing the rock, Gyas commanded his pilot Menoetes to hug the turn. But cautious Menoetes steered wide. Gyas raged as Cloanthus, taking the inside line, swept past the mark and into the lead. Mad with fury, Gyas seized the old pilot and hurled him overboard, then grabbed the helm himself and steered closer in.

The crowd laughed to see old Menoetes haul himself onto the rock, spitting seawater and gasping. Meanwhile, the Centaur and Dolphin gained hope. Sergestus tried to squeeze between his rival and the rock, but the Centaur struck the reef and shattered her oars. Mnestheus in the Dolphin, seizing his chance, urged his crew: "Pull, men! You who followed me from Troy's burning walls, show that same strength now! I don't ask for first place, though if only... but let us at least avoid the shame of coming last!" They rowed with desperate fury, and the Dolphin surged forward. He passed the stranded Centaur, then overtook Gyas's pilotless ship. Only Cloanthus remained ahead. Mnestheus bore down on him. The crowd screamed encouragement. Cloanthus, refusing to surrender the prize he already held, stretched his hands to the sea and prayed: "Gods of the deep, if you give me the victory, I will sacrifice a white bull and pour wine into your waves!" The nymphs and old Portunus himself pushed the Scylla forward. She flew to the harbor like an arrow and won the race.

Aeneas crowned Cloanthus with laurel and gave him three fat steers, wine, and a silver talent. Each captain received a rich embroidered cloak. Cloanthus's showed Ganymede being snatched by Jupiter's eagle. The frightened boy's guards stare upward helplessly while the dogs bark at the empty sky.

Mnestheus won the second prize: a coat of mail that Aeneas had stripped from the mighty Demoleus in single combat at Troy. Two servants could barely lift it, yet Demoleus had worn it while running down Trojans. The third-place captain received silver bowls and bronze cauldrons. Even Sergestus, who had wrecked his galley, was rewarded for saving his ship, limping home under one bank of oars like a wounded snake dragging its crushed coils.

The footrace came next. Nisus and his beloved companion Euryalus entered, along with Diores of Priam's line, Salius, Patron, two young Sicilian hunters named Helymus and Panopes, and many others. Aeneas announced the prizes: Cretan javelin-darts for all, olive wreaths for the top three, a horse for first, an Amazon's quiver for second, and a Greek helmet for third.

They took their marks and launched at the signal. Nisus burst into the lead, faster than wind or lightning. Salius came second, then Euryalus, then Helymus with Diores pressing at his shoulder. But near the finish, Nisus slipped in a pool of sacrificial blood and crashed to the ground. Even in his fall, he remembered his friend. As Salius came charging past, Nisus tripped him. Euryalus sprang over them both and crossed the line first, to thunderous applause. Helymus finished third and Diores fourth.

Salius protested furiously that he had been cheated. But the crowd loved handsome young Euryalus, and Diores backed them, not wanting Salius restored to third since that would cost him his own prize. Aeneas ruled: "The prizes stand as won, but let me compensate the unlucky." He gave Salius a magnificent lion's hide. Then Nisus, covered in mud and blood, grinned and said: "If losers get consolation prizes, what about me? I would have won if not for that puddle." Aeneas laughed and gave him a splendid shield.
"Now," Aeneas announced, "if any man dares test his courage in the boxing ring, let him step forward. A gilded bull for the winner, a sword and helmet to console the loser."

Dares stood up at once: a massive, fearless fighter who had once gone toe-to-toe with the giant Butes at Hector's funeral and knocked him dead on the sand. He swaggered to the center, flexed his huge arms, and threw punches at the air. No one dared face him. After waiting, he seized the bull by the horns and addressed Aeneas: "If nobody will fight me, how long must I stand here? Let me take my prize." The crowd roared its agreement.

Old Acestes was embarrassed. He nudged Entellus, a retired champion who sat watching. "Are you going to let this Trojan walk away with the prize unchallenged? Where is the spirit of Eryx, your teacher? Where is the fame that once filled this island?" Entellus shrugged: "My courage hasn't faded, but my blood is cold and my limbs are slow. If I still had the youth this braggart boasts of, I wouldn't need a prize to make me fight."

Then Entellus stood and threw down two enormous ox-hide gauntlets, weighted with iron and lead, stiff with dried blood and brains. Dares stared at them in shock and backed away. Entellus said: "These were my brother Eryx's. He wore them against Hercules himself. If they're too heavy, let us fight with equal gloves." Aeneas provided matched gauntlets. They squared off.

Entellus stripped off his quilted coat. Beneath it he was enormous: a tower of bone and muscle. Aeneas supplied equal gloves for both fighters. They squared off on tiptoe, arms raised, heads pulled back. Dares relied on youth and speed. Entellus on size and power. Blow after blow clanged against their helmets. The old fighter's breath came in heavy gasps, but his fists never stopped swinging. Dares ducked and circled. At last Entellus swung a mighty overhead blow that missed. His own momentum carried him crashing to the ground like a hollow pine torn from its roots. The crowd roared. Acestes helped his old friend to his feet. But Entellus rose transformed, burning with shame and fury. He drove Dares backward with a hailstorm of punches, left and right without pause, until Aeneas himself stepped in and stopped the fight. 'The gods favor him. Do not contend with divine strength.' Dares was carried away, spitting blood and broken teeth.

Entellus stood over the bull, his prize. "See what strength I once had," he told the crowd, "and what fate you saved Dares from." He drew back his fist and drove it straight through the bull's skull. The animal crashed to the ground, dead from one blow. "Eryx, accept this better sacrifice than Dares' blood. I lay down my gauntlets and retire from the ring."
Aeneas awarded the prizes with impartial justice. Dares received the promised sword and helmet as consolation. The other victors took their laurels and their gifts with pride.

For the archery contest, Aeneas raised the mast of Sergestus's wrecked ship on shore and tied a fluttering dove to the top. Lots were drawn. Hippocoon shot first and struck the mast. The frightened bird fluttered wildly. Mnestheus aimed higher but only cut the cord that held the dove. Free at last, she soared for the clouds. But Eurytion already had his arrow nocked. He prayed to his brother Apollo and let fly. The shaft caught her in mid-flight, and she tumbled to earth with the arrow still in her. Only Acestes remained, with no target left. He shot his arrow skyward. It caught fire as it flew, tracing a fiery trail across the sky before burning out. Trojans and Sicilians stared in wonder. Aeneas embraced the old king and declared it an omen from heaven. He gave Acestes a golden goblet that had once belonged to his own father.

Then came the riding display. Aeneas had young Ascanius lead three squadrons of boys on horseback. They rode out in beautiful formation, helmets gleaming, cornel-wood spears in hand, golden chains swinging at their chests.

They rode out in beautiful formation, helmets gleaming, cornel-wood spears in hand, golden chains swinging at their chests. Three captains led: young Priam, grandson of the old king, riding a white-spotted Thracian horse; handsome Atys, Ascanius's closest friend, leading the second troop; and Ascanius himself, radiant on a fiery Tyrian steed that Dido had given him. The rest rode Sicilian horses with golden bits.

Before the games were finished, Aeneas sent for Ascanius's tutor Periphantes and told him to bring out the boys if they were ready. The field was cleared. The noble youths rode out in gleaming formation, their fathers watching with swelling pride from every side.
The watching parents beamed with pride, seeing their own features reflected in their children.

The boys paraded before their fathers, then at a signal split into three troops, charged, wheeled, and regrouped. They advanced and retreated, threw harmless darts, and wove intricate patterns like the Cretan labyrinth. They were like dolphins playing through the waves. Ascanius later taught these games at Alba Longa, and from there the Romans inherited the tradition, calling it the Game of Troy.

But Fortune soon resumed her hostility. While the games continued, Juno sent rainbow-winged Iris down to the shore where the Trojan women sat weeping by the ships, mourning Anchises and lamenting the endless voyage. "How many seas remain?" they cried. "How much more must we endure?"

Iris disguised herself as old Beroe and slipped among the women. She urged them: "We wretches, whom not even Greece and fire could destroy, now endure seven years of storm and exile, searching for an Italy that always retreats before us. Here on this friendly shore, what stops us from building our own walls? Cassandra herself appeared in my dream and gave me torches, saying: 'This is your Troy! Here are your fated homes!' The time is now. See, Neptune's own altar fires will supply the brands!" She seized a firebrand and hurled it at the nearest ship.

Wise old Pyrgo saw through the disguise: "This is no Beroe! Look at her blazing eyes, her divine bearing! I just left the real Beroe, sick in bed." The women wavered between fear and longing. Then Iris revealed herself, soaring away on her rainbow arc. The sight drove the women mad. Screaming, they snatched brands from the altars and hurled them at the ships. Fire leaped from ship to ship, consuming paint and timber, oars and sails. Young Ascanius, still on horseback from the cavalry display, galloped up and cried: "What madness is this? You are burning your own hopes, not enemy ships! Look, it is your own Ascanius!" He threw down his helmet so they could see his face. Aeneas and the men came running. The shamed women scattered into the woods.

The fires were not easily quenched. They crept through the seams of the planking, smoldering beneath the surface, eating through oakum and pitch with patient malice. Smoke poured from the keels. The flames advanced upward to the masts and downward to the ballast. Neither buckets of water nor the strength of human hands could master the relentless element.
But the fires kept burning. The flames crept through the caulking and timber, smoke pouring from the keels. Water and human hands could not stop the fire.

Aeneas tore his robe and raised his hands to heaven: "Jupiter! If you do not utterly hate the Trojans, if any pity remains, save our fleet from the flames. Or else strike me dead with your thunderbolt and end it all here."
Instantly, a tremendous storm broke overhead. Rain poured down in sheets, flooding the decks and quenching the fires. Four ships were destroyed, but the rest were saved.

Aeneas was torn. Should he stay in Sicily and forget Italy? Old Nautes, the wisest of his counselors, advised him: "Bear what comes with patience, and press on when fortune favors you. Leave the weak, the old, the weary, and the faint-hearted here with Acestes. Build them a city and call it Acesta. Take only the brave young warriors with you to Italy."

That night, Anchises' ghost appeared to Aeneas in a dream. He confirmed Nautes's advice. "Take the bravest to Italy," he said. "The people there are tough and warlike. But first, you must visit me in the underworld. Come to Cumae and seek the Sibyl. She will guide you through the halls of Dis. I dwell not among the damned, but in the green fields of Elysium. There you will learn the fates of your descendants and the destiny of your line. Now farewell. Dawn approaches, and I must go." He faded like smoke. "Father, why do you flee my embrace?" Aeneas cried after him.

Aeneas woke, rekindled the sacred fire, and made offerings to the gods. Then he told his friends and Acestes his plan. They sorted the company. The timid and weary stayed behind. Aeneas laid out a city with the plow, assigned land by lot, and built a temple to Venus on Mount Eryx. A priest was appointed for Anchises' tomb. Nine days of feasting followed. Then a gentle breeze curled the sea and called the sailors aboard.

There were tears on both sides as the settlers and the sailors said goodbye. Even the women who had feared the sea now wished they could sail. Aeneas comforted them and commended them to Acestes' care. He sacrificed three calves on Eryx's altar and a lamb to the sea. Then he stood on the high stern, crowned with olive, poured the entrails into the waves, and made a libation of wine. Fresh winds filled the sails, and the fleet flew over the waves.

Venus, anxious as ever, went to Neptune and begged for safe passage for her son. She recounted all of Juno's persecutions: the storm off Libya, the burning of the ships, the endless wandering. "My son is sailing for Latium. Grant him the safety of your seas." Neptune smiled: "Venus, you were born from my waves. You have every right to trust me. I have protected Aeneas before, when Achilles was slaughtering Trojans on the banks of the Xanthus and the river was choked with bodies. I wrapped Aeneas in cloud and carried him to safety, even though I longed to see ungrateful Troy destroyed. I will do the same now. Your fleet will reach Italy safely. Only one life is owed to the sea, one man given for the many." He harnessed his sea-horses, calmed the waves, and rode across the surface. The tempests fled before him. Tritons and sea-nymphs escorted him, and the ocean lay smooth as glass.

Aeneas ordered every sail raised. They raced through the calm sea. Night came. The god of Sleep descended from the stars, wearing the shape of Phorbas, and settled on the prow beside the helmsman Palinurus. "The wind is steady," Sleep whispered. "The ships sail themselves. Close your eyes for just an hour. I will take the helm." Palinurus refused: "You ask me to trust the treacherous sea? To hand over the fleet to a calm that could change in a heartbeat? Never." He gripped the tiller and fixed his gaze on the stars. But the god shook a branch dipped in the river of forgetfulness over him. Palinurus's eyes grew heavy. Before he could fight it, Sleep shoved him headlong into the sea, tearing the rudder away with him. The pilot fell, calling for help that never came. The god of Sleep flew off, and the fleet sailed on unharmed, as Neptune had promised. They passed the Sirens' rocks, white with the bones of sailors, and the sound of crashing waves. Aeneas, sensing his ship was drifting, took the helm himself and steered through the dark night, mourning his lost friend: "O Palinurus, you trusted too much in a calm sea and a clear sky. You will lie unburied on a foreign shore."

chapters.title: Book VI
paragraphs: The Sibyl foretells the struggles Aeneas will face in Italy. She guides him down to the underworld, showing him its many regions and conducting him to his father Anchises, who reveals the great philosophical mysteries of the world-soul and reincarnation, and shows him the glorious line of heroes destined to descend from him.

Weeping, Aeneas spread his sails and reached the shores of Cumae. They anchored the fleet and went ashore. Some struck sparks from flint to kindle fires. Others gathered wood or traced the courses of streams. But Aeneas climbed the sacred hill where Apollo's temple stood, with its golden roof, and sought the cave of the dread Sibyl. The temple's doors were carved by Daedalus himself, who had flown from Crete on jointed wings and landed here. He carved the death of Androgeos, the Athenian youths sent as tribute, the labyrinth, Ariadne's thread, and the Minotaur's defeat. He tried twice to carve his son Icarus's fall, but grief stayed his hand each time.

While Aeneas marveled at these carvings, the Sibyl's priestess arrived: Deiphobe, daughter of Glaucus. "This is no time for sightseeing," she said. "Sacrifice seven bulls to Apollo and seven ewes to Diana." They obeyed. She led them to the cave: a vast opening with a hundred mouths, from which a hundred voices poured the Sibyl's prophecies. At the threshold, she cried: "Now is the time! Ask your fate! The god is here!" Her face changed. Her hair stood on end. She trembled and grew larger than mortal size, as Apollo seized her soul.

Aeneas prayed to Apollo with his hands raised: "O god, you guided the Trojan arrow that struck Achilles' mortal heel. You have led me through every sea and savage land. Now that at last we have reached Italy's shore, let the curse of Troy pursue us no further. Grant me a home in Latium for my wandering gods and people. I will build you a temple and establish a priesthood to guard your oracles forever. But do not write your prophecies on leaves for the winds to scatter. Speak them aloud."

The Sibyl resisted the god's power, struggling beneath his weight. But Apollo forced his way into her soul, taming her frenzy. The cave's hundred doors burst open, and her voice rang out: "You have escaped the dangers of the sea, but worse waits on land. The Trojans will reach Latium, but they will wish they had not. I see wars, terrible wars. The Tiber running with blood. A new Achilles awaits you, also born of a goddess. Juno will never stop persecuting you. You will beg for help from every quarter, driven by a foreign bride and a foreign war. But do not yield. Press on with greater courage. Your first deliverance will come from where you least expect it: a Greek city."

The Sibyl spoke these dark warnings from her cave, wrapping truth in riddles. Apollo drove her hard, and the cave shook with thunder. At last the frenzy ebbed. Aeneas said: "Nothing you tell me is unexpected. I have prepared myself for every danger. But grant me one thing. They say the gate to the underworld lies nearby. Let me descend and see my father. He appeared in my dreams and urged me to come. Orpheus brought back his wife from hell. Pollux shares his life between the upper and lower worlds. Theseus and Hercules both went down and returned. I am descended from Jupiter, no less than they."

The Sibyl replied: "Son of Anchises, the descent to the underworld is easy. The gates of death stand open night and day. But to climb back to the upper world, that is the great labor. Few have managed it, and only those of divine blood or exceptional virtue. Between here and there lie deep forests and impenetrable night. But if your love for your father drives you to brave such danger, here is what you must do. In a dark wood nearby, hidden from sight, grows a tree with a single branch of gold. This golden bough is sacred to Proserpine, Queen of the Dead. You must find it and pluck it. If fate favors you, it will come away easily. If not, no force can tear it free. But first, one of your companions lies dead and unburied, polluting your fleet. Attend to his funeral before you attempt the journey below."

Aeneas left the cave, heavy with sorrow, wondering who the dead man was. He and Achates walked in silence, speculating. Soon they found the body of Misenus lying on the shore. He had been a great trumpeter who served Hector and then Aeneas. But he had foolishly challenged the sea-god Triton, who drowned him. The Trojans wept and set about building a funeral pyre. They felled pines, oaks, and ash trees on the mountainside. Aeneas worked alongside his men.

As he labored, Aeneas prayed to Venus for help finding the golden bough. Two doves, his mother's birds, descended and led him through the forest. They flew from tree to tree, stopping to feed, always staying just ahead. At last they landed on a tree where a gleam of gold shone through the green leaves. It was the golden bough, glittering like mistletoe on a winter oak. Aeneas seized it and tore it away. It came easily. He carried it back to the Sibyl. Meanwhile, his men completed Misenus's funeral. They burned the pyre, washed the bones, and sealed them in a bronze urn. Aeneas raised a tomb on the headland, topped with the dead man's trumpet, oar, and spear. The place still bears Misenus's name. Then Aeneas turned to the descent. The cave entrance gaped, guarded by a dark grove. No bird could fly over the poisonous lake at its foot. The Sibyl sacrificed four black bulls, a lamb to Hecate, and a barren heifer to Proserpine. As dawn approached, the earth groaned, trees shook, and spectral dogs howled. "Stand back, all who are not worthy!" the Sibyl cried. "Aeneas, draw your sword and follow me. Now is the time for courage." She plunged into the darkness, and he followed.
O gods of the underworld, silent shades, permit me to tell what I saw in your dark kingdom.
They walked through the gloom like travelers in a wood under a failing moon, when Jupiter has hidden the sky in cloud and darkness drains the color from all things.

Just inside the gates of hell, they found Grief, Anxiety, Disease, Old Age, Fear, Hunger, and Poverty standing guard. Beside them lurked Death and his brother Sleep, guilty Pleasures, War, the Furies on their iron beds, and Discord with snakes in her hair. In the center stood a great elm where empty Dreams clung to every leaf. Beyond it, monsters waited: Centaurs, Gorgons, the hundred-handed Briareus, the Hydra, and the fire-breathing Chimaera. Aeneas drew his sword, but the Sibyl told him these were only hollow phantoms. They pressed on to the banks of Acheron, a muddy, churning river. There stood Charon, the grim boatman, ancient and filthy, with burning eyes. He ferried crowds of the dead across the water. But not all were admitted. Husbands, wives, children, heroes, all pressed forward with outstretched hands, but Charon accepted some and turned others away. Aeneas asked the Sibyl why. She explained that only those who had received proper burial could cross. The unburied must wander the shore for a hundred years.

"These rejected ghosts," the Sibyl said, "have been denied burial. Charon only ferries those whose bones have been properly laid to rest. The others must wander a hundred years before they can cross." Aeneas recognized among them his lost companions from the storm. He also saw Leucaspis and the captain of the Lycian crew, whose ships had been overwhelmed.

Then Palinurus appeared, still fresh from his recent death. He told Aeneas how Sleep had overcome him, how he had clung to the broken rudder, and how, after three days adrift, he had reached the Italian shore only to be murdered by the savage inhabitants. His body was tossed back into the waves. He begged Aeneas to take him across. But the Sibyl said: "That is forbidden. But take comfort: the people who killed you will be punished by heaven, and a tomb bearing your name will be raised there." Palinurus was consoled by the promise of lasting fame.

They approached the Stygian lake. Charon saw them and shouted: "Stop! This is the realm of the dead. No living man may board my boat. I had trouble enough when Hercules dragged Cerberus away, and when Theseus and Pirithous tried to steal Proserpine." The Sibyl answered calmly: "We mean no harm. This is Aeneas, son of Venus, famous for his devotion. He seeks his father in Elysium. If piety and heaven's command do not move you, then look at this." She revealed the golden bough. Charon's anger dissolved. He cleared his boat of ghosts and took Aeneas aboard. The leaky vessel groaned under the living man's weight but carried them across.

On the far shore, they faced three-headed Cerberus, bristling with snakes. The Sibyl threw him a drugged honey cake. He gulped it down and collapsed in sleep, filling the cavern with his sprawled bulk. They hurried past. Beyond him lay the regions of the dead, sorted by the manner of their dying. First, innocent babies, snatched too soon. Then those condemned unjustly, judged now by Minos. Then suicides, who longed too late for the life they had thrown away.

Next they reached the Mourning Fields, where souls destroyed by love wandered in myrtle groves. Among them, Aeneas found Dido. He could barely see her through the gloom. Tears filled his eyes. "Unhappy queen, so the news of your death was true, and I was the cause. I swear by heaven and by the powers below, I left your shore unwillingly. The gods commanded me. I never imagined my departure would bring you to this. Stay. Let me see you. This is the last time fate allows us to speak." But Dido would not look at him. She stared at the ground as if he were a stone. Then she turned and fled into the shadows, where her husband Sichaeus waited to return her love.

Aeneas wept and moved on. He came to the fields where the warrior souls dwell. Dead Trojan heroes flocked around him joyfully, but the Greek shades fled in terror at the sight of his shining armor, just as they had fled from him in life.

He found Deiphobus, Priam's son, horribly disfigured. His face was slashed, his ears and nose cut off, his hands mutilated. Aeneas barely recognized him. Deiphobus told how his treacherous wife Helen, on Troy's last night, had hidden his sword, opened the door to the Greeks, and let Menelaus and Ulysses murder him in his sleep. He asked Aeneas what brought a living man to the underworld.

Deiphobus's ghost replied: "Your devotion has given my wandering shade all the rites it needs. My fate was sealed by my own cruel wife. On the last night of Troy, while I lay exhausted from the celebrations, Helen removed every weapon from the house and stole the sword from beneath my pillow. Then she opened the door and called in Menelaus and Ulysses, hoping to win back her husband's favor with this gift. They burst in and murdered me in my sleep. They slashed my face, cut off my ears and nose. I barely recognized myself. But why go on? You know that Helen's treachery matched her beauty. But tell me of yourself. What brings a living man to this dark shore? Is it the wandering of the seas, or a command from heaven?"

But the Sibyl interrupted: "Night is passing. We waste time in tears. The road divides here. The right path leads to Elysium, the home of the blessed. The left descends to Tartarus, where the wicked suffer their punishments." Deiphobus said farewell: "Do not be angry, great priestess. I will return to my place among the shades. Go, our glory, go and enjoy a better fate than mine." He spoke, and with those words turned away into the darkness.

Aeneas looked to the left and saw a fortress surrounded by a river of fire. From within came the crack of whips, the clank of chains, and terrible groans. He asked the Sibyl what crimes were punished there.

She told him: "No pure soul may enter Tartarus. But when Hecate made me priestess of these groves, she showed me its horrors. Rhadamanthus rules that place. He forces every soul to confess its hidden crimes. The Fury lashes them with serpents and summons her sisters. The brazen gates grind open. Inside, the Hydra watches with fifty gaping mouths. The pit drops twice as deep as the sky is high above the earth. Here lie the Titans, struck down by Jupiter's lightning. Here Tityus, whose liver is eternally devoured by a vulture. Here Ixion on his wheel, and Tantalus forever reaching for food that retreats. Here are those who betrayed their brothers, beat their parents, defrauded their dependents, hoarded gold, committed adultery, started wars for pay, and sold their country's freedom. Their punishments are beyond my power to describe. But we must press on. I see Pluto's palace. This is where you must place the golden bough."

They walked through the gathering gloom to the palace gates. Aeneas sprinkled himself with fresh water and fixed the golden bough above the entrance. With these rites performed, they entered the Blessed Fields: Elysium. A purple sky with its own sun and stars arched above green meadows. Happy souls exercised, wrestled, danced, and sang. The Thracian poet Orpheus played his seven-stringed lyre among them. Here were the founders of Troy: Assaracus, Ilus, and Dardanus himself. Aeneas saw their chariots and their horses, free of their harness, grazing on the eternal grass. Other souls feasted beneath laurel trees, singing joyfully. Here were patriots who died for their country, priests who led blameless lives, poets beloved by the gods, inventors whose arts enriched the world, and all who earned remembrance through kindness.

The Sibyl asked the greatest of these blessed souls, the poet Musaeus, where to find Anchises. "The happy souls have no fixed dwelling," he replied. "We live in groves and meadows by crystal streams. But come, follow me up this hill, and I will show you the way." He led them up and pointed to the shining fields below.

Anchises stood in a flowering valley, reviewing the souls destined to be born into the world. He was studying each one, noting their names, their fates, their future deeds. When he saw Aeneas approaching, tears of joy streamed down his face. "Welcome, my son! I knew you would come. The love and devotion that drove you through such dangers have not disappointed me. What seas you have crossed, what perils survived! And how I feared for you on the Libyan coast." Aeneas reached out to embrace him, but three times his arms closed on empty air, light as wind or a fleeting dream.

In a hidden valley, Aeneas saw the river Lethe, where crowds of souls swarmed like bees over summer flowers. He asked what they were doing. Anchises explained: "These are souls fated for new bodies. They drink from Lethe to forget their former lives before they are reborn. I have long wanted to show you your glorious descendants, so that you might rejoice in Italy all the more." "Father," Aeneas asked, "can it be that souls freed by death would willingly return to sluggish bodies?"

Anchises answered with a great philosophical teaching. He explained that a single divine spirit animates all of nature: heaven, earth, sea, moon, sun, and stars. This universal soul, mixed with matter, produces men, beasts, birds, and sea creatures. But the earthly body weighs down the divine spark. Imprisoned in flesh, the soul suffers desire, fear, grief, and joy, and cannot see its own heavenly nature. Even death does not wash away all stains. The accumulated filth of life clings to the soul. Some are cleansed by wind, some by water, some by fire. After ages of purification, the few who achieve perfect purity breathe the air of Elysium. The rest, after a thousand years, are herded to the river Lethe to drink forgetfulness, so they can be born again into mortal bodies.

Then Anchises led his son and the Sibyl to a high point overlooking the procession of future souls. "Look," he said. "These are the Italian heroes whose blood will mingle with yours. See Silvius, your last-born son, whom Lavinia will raise in the forests. He will be the first of a line of Alban kings. After him come Procas, Capys, Numitor, and another Silvius Aeneas. See the men with oak-leaf crowns who will found Gabii, Fidenae, Nomentum, and Collatia. And there is Romulus, born of Mars, who will build Rome's walls. Under him, Rome's power will match the earth, and her spirit will rival the gods. Her seven hills will be crowned with towers.

"Now see the Julian line. There is Caesar Augustus himself, promised so long, destined to restore the Golden Age. His empire will stretch beyond India, beyond the paths of the sun. Before him, even the prophets of Egypt tremble. No hero, not even Hercules or Bacchus, traveled farther or achieved more. And there, crowned with olive, is Numa, the second king, who will give Rome her sacred laws. After him, warlike Tullus, then Ancus. See the Tarquin kings, and Brutus the liberator, who will execute his own sons for treason, placing country above family. There are the Decii, the Drusi, Camillus who saved Rome's standards from the Gauls. And there, sadly, are Caesar and Pompey, father-in-law and son-in-law, destined to turn their armies against each other in civil war. Others may cast bronze more gracefully, plead law more eloquently, or chart the stars more precisely. But Rome, your art is to rule the peoples of the world, to impose the ways of peace, to spare the conquered, and to crush the proud. These are your imperial arts."

He paused, then pointed to a magnificent figure: "There is Marcellus, who will defeat the Gauls in single combat and offer the third great spoils to Jupiter." Beside him walked a beautiful young man in gleaming armor, but his eyes were downcast and his brow was shadowed. "Who is he?" Aeneas asked. Anchises wept: "Do not ask, my son. Fate will barely show him to the world before snatching him away. The gods judged that Rome's power would grow too great if such a gift were allowed to last. How the warriors will weep! What funeral processions will line the Tiber! No Roman youth will ever raise such hopes or cause such grief. If only you could break through fate's harsh decree! Scatter lilies and purple roses. Let me honor this lost boy with flowers, a vain and useless gift." Then Anchises led his son through the rest of Elysium, showed him the future wars, and taught him how to face what lay ahead.

There are two gates of Sleep. One is made of polished ivory, through which false dreams pass. The other is of transparent horn, through which true visions come. Anchises led them to the ivory gate and sent them through it back to the upper world. Aeneas went straight to his ships, embarked his men, and sailed along the coast until he reached the bay of Caieta. There they anchored, with their sterns to shore.

chapters.title: Book VII
paragraphs: King Latinus welcomes Aeneas and promises him his only daughter Lavinia. But Turnus, who loves Lavinia and is favored by her mother, breaks the treaty. Juno sends the Fury Alecto to stir up war. Turnus rallies the neighboring princes and their armies against the Trojans. The forces of Italy and their commanders are described in detail.
And you, Cajeta, noble nurse of great Aeneas, gave your name to this shore when you died here. Your bones rest in the rich Italian plains. Your name, which is all a ghost can keep, lives on.

When Aeneas had honored Cajeta with funeral rites, he sailed on through the Tyrrhenian Sea. A gentle night breeze filled his sails. The stars shone bright, the moon silvered the water. They passed the dangerous coast of Circe, the Sun's rich daughter. They could hear from her island the roaring of caged lions, the grunting of bristled boars, the growling of bears, and the howling of wolves. These were men whom Circe's magic had transformed into beasts. But Neptune sent favorable winds that carried the Trojans safely past. At dawn, the wind fell calm. From the ship, Aeneas saw a great forest, and flowing through it, the river Tiber, rolling its yellow current to the sea. Birds sang in the branches along its banks. Aeneas gave the order to turn inland. The joyful crew steered through the shadows of the trees and left the open sea behind.

Now, Erato, inspire my song! Tell me what Latium was, who its ancient kings were, and what state of things the Trojans found when their fleet first touched the Italian shore. I will sing of battles, of blood and rage, of proud nations driven to war, of all Italy called to arms. A greater story begins here, and a greater labor.

Old King Latinus had long ruled the Latin people in peace. His father was Faunus, his grandfather Picus, and his ancestor Saturn himself. But heaven had given Latinus no son. His boys had died young, leaving only one daughter, Lavinia, to inherit the throne. Many neighboring princes sought her hand. The most prominent was Turnus, handsome and noble, favored by Queen Amata. But terrible omens forbade the match.

In the heart of the palace grew an ancient laurel tree, sacred to Apollo, which Latinus had found when he first built his city walls. One day a swarm of bees descended from the sky and clustered on its topmost branch. An old seer prophesied: "A foreign prince will come from the same direction as these bees. His army will land on our shores, conquer the city, and rule from its towers."

There was more. While Lavinia stood beside her father at the altar, feeding the sacred fire, the flames suddenly caught her hair and her jeweled crown. Fire ran crackling through her ornaments and spread across her royal robes, wrapping her head in a halo of light and smoke. The seer declared: "This maiden will be famous and glorious, but her fate will bring war and devastation to the nation."

Alarmed by these portents, Latinus went to consult his father Faunus at the oracle near Albunea's sulfurous spring. Priests slept on the hides of sacrificed sheep in the sacred grove, and in their dreams received visions from the powers above and below. Latinus sacrificed a hundred sheep, lay down on the fleeces, and in his sleep heard a voice: "Do not seek a Latin husband for your daughter, my son. A foreign prince will come whose descendants will rule the world, whose fame will reach the stars." This prophecy spread through the neighboring lands just as the Trojan fleet came into view.

Beneath a shady tree, Aeneas spread a simple meal on the grass: flat cakes of bread topped with forest fruits. When they had eaten everything, hungry Ascanius laughed and said: "Look, we are even eating our tables!" The word struck Aeneas like a thunderbolt. This was the prophecy his father Anchises had spoken: "When hunger drives you to eat your very tables, you will know you have found your home." Aeneas leaped to his feet. "Hail, promised land! Hail, household gods! This is our destined place. This is where our labor ends. Tomorrow we will explore this country. Today, let us feast and give thanks to the gods." He crowned his cup and poured to Jupiter, then to his father's spirit.

He wreathed his brow with branches and sacrificed to the genius of the place, to Earth, to the nymphs, to Night and the rising stars, to Cybele, and to Jupiter above and Venus below. Jupiter answered with three peals of thunder and shook a golden cloud. Word flew through the camp: the time had come to build their city. Every brow was crowned with green, and the feasting redoubled.

The next morning, scouts went out in all directions to map the coastline, the rivers, and the settlements. Aeneas selected a hundred of his best men, wreathed their heads with olive branches, and sent them as ambassadors to King Latinus's palace, carrying gifts and asking for peace. Meanwhile, he began laying out his camp, digging trenches and building ramparts.

The ambassadors approached the city and saw Latin youths training on the dusty plain: some driving chariots, some riding horses, some bending bows. A messenger ran ahead to tell the king that tall foreigners in strange clothing had arrived. Latinus ordered them admitted and took his seat on the royal throne.

The palace of Picus was magnificent: a vast hall supported by a hundred pillars, surrounded by a sacred wood. Here kings received their scepters and senators feasted. Along the entrance stood carved wooden statues of the royal ancestors: old Saturn with his sickle, Italus the founder, ancient two-faced Janus with his keys, good Sabinus the vine-planter, and warlike kings with honorable battle wounds. Helmets, shields, broken ship-prows, and captured chariots hung from the columns. At the head of them all sat Picus himself, holding a buckler and a divining wand, dressed in his priestly robes. Circe had once loved him, and when he refused her, she transformed him into a woodpecker with bright feathers.

In this temple, Latinus received the Trojans from his chair of state. He spoke kindly: "Tell me, Trojans, for we know your name and your voyage is no secret. What brings you here? Were you driven off course by storms, or do you seek our harbors deliberately? Whatever the cause, the Latins are a welcoming people by nature, not by force. We follow Saturn's ancient custom of hospitality. I recall an old tale that Dardanus, your ancestor, was born in these very lands before he sailed to Phrygia."

Ilioneus replied: "Great king, no storms forced us here. We came deliberately, exiles from the greatest city the sun ever shone upon. Jupiter himself began our line, and Jupiter's command drives us to your shores. We have been tossed across every sea since Troy fell. All we ask is a small piece of land, water, and air, things you will not miss. We will not disgrace your kingdom. Many nations have sought alliance with us. Do not scorn us because we come as suppliants with olive branches. Fate and the gods have destined us for Latium. Here Dardanus was born, and here Apollo sends us. We bring gifts: this golden bowl Anchises used for sacrifice, this robe and crown that Priam wore, this scepter, these purple garments woven by Trojan women."

Latinus listened in silence, his eyes fixed on the ground. He was thinking not of the gifts but of something far greater: succession, empire, his daughter's fate. This must be the foreign prince the omens foretold. At last he raised his head and spoke: "May the gods bless us both! You shall have what you ask. Take land where you please, and share my kingdom. Tell your king not to send ambassadors but to come himself. Let me embrace him as a friend. I have one daughter, whom heaven and fate forbid me to give to any native prince. A foreigner is destined to come, a great warrior, whose descendants will carry the Latin name to glory. I believe your Aeneas is that man."

He gave each ambassador a caparisoned horse from his royal stables, three hundred in all, with purple trappings and golden bits. For Aeneas himself, he sent a chariot drawn by a pair of horses bred from immortal stock, stolen by Circe from the Sun-god's herd. The ambassadors rode home with peace and gifts.

But jealous Juno, flying from Argos past the headland of Pachynus, looked down and saw the Trojans already settled, building their camp, and the ambassadors returning with a treaty of peace. Pierced with rage, she cried: "O hated race! O fates of Troy that war with mine! Could they not die on the plains, or burn with their city? Through fire and sword and sea they found their way. My power is spent, my fury exhausted. I chased them across every ocean, hurled storms and waves at them, and still they thrive. Mars could bathe the Centaurs in blood, Jupiter let Diana destroy Calydon. But I, queen of heaven, have been defeated by a mortal man. Very well. If I cannot prevent the marriage, I can at least delay it. If heaven denies me, hell will serve. I cannot stop the fates, but I can drench the wedding in blood. Both nations shall pay dearly, and the bride's dowry will be the ruin of Trojans and Latins alike."

She plunged through the earth to the gates of hell and summoned Alecto, a Fury so hideous that even her own sisters despised her. Juno inflamed the monster's spite: "Daughter of Night, do me this service. Prevent the Trojans from winning the Latin king with their false peace. Shatter the treaty. Sow discord. Kindle blood against blood and fill the land with war."

The Fury flew on dark wings to the Latin palace. She found Queen Amata restless and burning with resentment that Turnus had been set aside for a foreign stranger. Alecto plucked a poisonous snake from her own hair and slipped it into the queen's breast. The serpent wound invisibly between her garments and her skin, breathing its venom into her blood. At first the poison worked slowly. Amata went to her husband and pleaded with gentle tears: "Will you give our daughter to a wandering exile? Have you no pity for a mother? This Trojan pirate will steal her away, just as Paris stole Helen. What of your promise to Turnus? If you insist on a foreigner, then Turnus qualifies. Trace his lineage back far enough and you find he comes from Argive blood."

But Latinus would not budge. The snake's full poison took hold. Amata went mad. Like a spinning top lashed by boys in a courtyard, she whirled through the city and out into the wild woods, dragging Lavinia with her. She hid the girl among the forests, pretending to celebrate the rites of Bacchus. "Worthy of Bacchus alone!" she shrieked, leading the women in frenzied dance, shaking a pine torch and singing a wedding song for Turnus. The other mothers, seized by the same fury, abandoned their homes and streamed after her into the hills, their hair wild, their voices shrill.

Having driven Amata mad, the Fury flew to the city of Ardea, where young Turnus lay sleeping. She disguised herself as old Chalybe, a priestess of Juno, and appeared in his dream: "Turnus, will you let everything you fought for be given to a Trojan newcomer? The king breaks his promise. Go take what is yours by right. Juno herself commands it. Arm your men and burn the Trojan ships that squat in the Tiber's mouth." Turnus laughed at her: "Old woman, I know the fleet has arrived. I neither fear nor seek this war. Juno watches over me. Go back to your temple and leave war to men."

At that, Alecto dropped her disguise. Her eyes blazed with hellfire, her snakes writhed and hissed. She reared up and cracked her whip: "Look at me, old woman that I am! I carry war and death and destruction in my hands! Behold the Furies' minister!"

She hurled her smoking torch into his breast. He woke drenched in cold sweat, screaming for arms. His blood boiled like water in a seething cauldron. He called his men and sent messengers to every ally: prepare for war, defend Italy, drive out the invaders.

Meanwhile the Fury turned her attention to the Trojans. On a hilltop above the plain, she spotted young Ascanius hunting with hounds and horses. She fired the dogs with the scent of a great stag, a tame creature that belonged to the household of Tyrrheus, the king's chief ranger.

The two sons of Tyrrheus had raised this stag from a fawn, and their sister Silvia had tended it lovingly. She tied ribbons around its budding antlers, combed its silky coat, and bathed it. The trusting animal grazed in the forest by day and came home to its known lodging each night.

This gentle creature was what Ascanius's dogs now chased. The boy drew his bow, and the Fury guided the fatal arrow. It pierced the stag's side. Bleeding and groaning, the wounded animal stumbled home. Silvia screamed for help. The country folk came running with clubs and burning brands. Tyrrheus himself snatched a hatchet. Alecto, perched on a barn roof, blew a blast on a shepherd's horn so terrible that it echoed across the hills and lakes. Mothers clutched their babies in fright.

The country people charged out in a mob. The Trojans rushed to support Ascanius. What began with clubs and firebrands quickly escalated to swords and shields. It was like a rising sea: first white foam on the waves, then a full storm that churns mud from the ocean floor. Young Almon, eldest son of Tyrrheus, was the first killed, an arrow in his throat. Old Galesus, the richest farmer in Latium, a man of peace, fell too, cut down while trying to calm the fighting.

When she had bathed both sides in blood, the Fury flew to Juno. "Your war is begun," she said. "The blood is drawn, the discord sealed. Shall I spread the fire to the neighboring nations?" Juno dismissed her: "Enough. The seeds of hatred are sown. You have done your work. Now return to hell. Leave the rest to me." The sullen Fury spread her wings and sank through a chasm in the earth called Lake Amsanctus, where black waters boil up from hell's mouth, surrounded by dark forests.

Juno herself now managed the war. The country people carried their dead into the city, crying for justice. Turnus was there, inflaming their rage, shouting that the king had broken his promise for a foreign mongrel. The Bacchic women, Amata's followers, added their voices. Against all omens and all reason, the mob demanded war. Old Latinus stood firm like a rock battered by waves. When he saw that Juno's power had overwhelmed every voice of reason, he withdrew. "You will pay for this madness," he told them. "And you, Turnus, will bear the heaviest punishment. My storms are over. I sail toward death in peace." He shut himself in his palace and refused to preside over the declaration of war.

There was an ancient custom in Latium: when war was declared, the king himself opened the iron-bolted gates of the Temple of Janus. Two doors of steel, guarded by the double-faced god, held back the fury of Mars. Latinus refused to open them. So Juno herself flew down from heaven, struck the bolts with her own hand, and burst the gates wide. War poured out like a tempest.

All peaceful Italy was ablaze. The cities that had drowsed in ease now forged weapons day and night. Some polished rusty shields, some sharpened axes and spears. Five cities rang with the sound of hammering: Atina, Tibur, Ardea, Antemnae, and Crustumerium. They hammered helmets, wove shields from willow, and melted down ploughshares into swords. The trumpet sounded, and men laced on their armor, embraced their shields, and mounted their horses.

Now open your Helicon, O Muses, and sing of the warriors who answered the call, the armies that filled the Italian plains. First came Mezentius, the despiser of the gods, exiled from Etruria, leading his baffled host to Turnus's aid. At his side rode his beautiful son Lausus, a fine horseman and hunter. He deserved a better father and a happier fate. A thousand men followed him.

Next came Aventinus, son of Hercules, driving his chariot crowned with palms and laurels. His shield bore the Hydra with a hundred hissing serpents. He was born on the Aventine Hill, where Hercules had stopped with his Spanish cattle. His men fought with long pikes and javelins. He himself wore a lion's skin and a shaggy mane, like his divine father.

Then the twin brothers Catillus and Coras rode down from Tibur, leading Argive cavalry. They charged into the front lines like cloud-born Centaurs crashing down a mountainside, scattering the forest before them.

Caeculus, founder of Praeneste, who was said to have been found in a fire and raised by shepherds, led a band of rustic soldiers from the Gabine country, from cold Anio, from the wet fields of Hernica. They had no proper armor. They slung lead balls from leather straps, wore cork helmets, and wrapped one foot in raw bull-hide. Beside them marched Messapus, son of Neptune, whom no fire or sword could kill. He led the men of Falisci, from Lake Ciminus and Feronia's groves. They marched in order and sang as they went, like a long formation of white swans flying high, their music echoing across the sky.

Then Clausus brought a mighty army from the Sabine country. He alone was worth an army. From him the noble Claudian family descended, which in later ages would share in Rome's greatness. He led the men of Cures, Amiternum, the craggy heights of Tetrica, and the banks of the Tiber, Himella, and Fabaris. They came in numbers thick as waves on the Libyan sea or stalks of grain on the Asian harvest fields. Their trampling shook the ground.

Halesus, son of Agamemnon, a born enemy of Troy, brought a thousand men from the Massic wine country, the Auruncan hills, and the banks of roaring Vulturnus. They threw light javelins on leather thongs and carried short curved swords and small round shields.
Oebalus, son of the nymph Semethis, led warriors from Capri and Campania. They wielded brazen swords and slung heavy stones. Their helmets were made of cork.
Ufens led the mountain men of Nursia, the tough Equicolae, who ploughed in armor and were always ready for battle. Their soil was barren and their hearts were hard.

Oebalus, son of the nymph Semethis and old Telon, came from the island of Capri. But the island was too small for his ambition. He had spread his rule across Campania, where the Sarnus river seeks the Tyrrhenian sea, and over Batulum and Abella with its orchards. His men fought in the old Teutonic style with bronze swords and bronze shields. They slung heavy stones from a distance and wore helmets of cork.

Next came the warlike Ufens, leading the mountain troops of Nursia. The rough Equicolae followed him. Their trade was hunting and plunder. They ploughed in armor and were always ready for battle. Their soil was barren and their hearts were as hard as the rocks they tilled.

Umbro the priest led the proud Marrubians, his head crowned with peaceful olive. He could charm vipers to sleep with his herbs and spells, but no Marsian magic could heal the wound the Trojan spear would give him. The forests of Angitia mourned, and the waters of Lake Fucinus wept for him.

Young Virbius came too, the son of the famous Hippolytus who had been torn apart by his own horses and then restored to life by Diana and the healer Aesculapius. Jupiter, outraged that a mortal should conquer death, struck the physician down with a thunderbolt. Diana hid the restored Hippolytus in her sacred grove and renamed him Virbius. For this reason, horses were forbidden from Trivia's temple. His son, the second Virbius, now drove his chariot to war.

High above them all rode Turnus himself, taller by a head than any man, his triple-plumed helmet crowned with a fire-breathing Chimera that blazed more fiercely as the battle rose. His shield bore the image of the maiden Io, transformed into a cow, watched by hundred-eyed Argus, while her father the river-god poured his stream from a silver urn. Behind him marched a vast infantry of Argives, Sicani, old Rutulians, Auruncans, Labicans, and men from every hill and stream of Latium.

Last of all came Camilla of the Volscians, a warrior maiden. She had never learned to spin or weave. She chose instead the arts of war and the speed of the wind. She could run across a field of standing grain without bending a single stalk, or skim the surface of the sea without wetting her feet. Men, women, and children gaped as she passed, devouring her with their eyes: her purple cloak, her golden hair-clasp, her myrtle javelin, and the Lycian quiver dancing at her back.

chapters.title: Book VIII
paragraphs: War has begun. Both sides prepare. Turnus sends to Diomedes for help. Aeneas travels in person to seek allies from Evander and the Tuscans. Evander receives him warmly, gives him soldiers, and sends his own son Pallas along. Venus persuades Vulcan to forge divine armor for Aeneas, and on the great shield the god engraves the most glorious deeds of Aeneas's future descendants.

When Turnus had raised his standard on Laurentum's towers and the trumpet had sounded across the land, the Latin youth rushed to arms. Fierce Ufens, Messapus, and blasphemous Mezentius swept through the countryside, ravaging fields and gathering forces. They sent Venulus to Diomedes the Greek, begging him to join the war against Aeneas: 'The Trojan has landed with his banished gods and claims a kingdom. Many nations rally to his name. What he intends, and what will follow if he succeeds, affects us all.'

While Turnus pressed the war, Aeneas lay awake, turning his anxious mind this way and that, unable to rest. His thoughts flashed back and forth like sunlight bouncing off a bowl of water, darting across walls and ceiling.

Night came at last. While every creature slept, Aeneas lay on the riverbank, heavy with care. In a vision, the god of the Tiber himself rose from the water, an old man in a blue robe with reeds crowning his head. He spoke: 'Long-awaited prince, who has carried Troy's gods to their promised home, this is the place. Do not fear the war. Juno's rage will pass. As proof this is no empty dream, you will find on the shore a white sow with thirty white piglets. In thirty years, your son Ascanius will build a great city called Alba. Listen: upstream from here, the Arcadian Evander has built a town called Pallanteum. He and the fierce Latins are already at war. Make him your ally. I will smooth my current to carry your ships upstream. When you return victorious, honor me with sacrifice. I am Tiber, the river of mighty Rome.'

The god plunged below. Aeneas woke, saw the dawn reddening the sky, and scooped water from the river to pray: 'Tiber, king of rivers, receive me and keep me safe. I will honor you every day.' He chose two galleys, manned them, and prepared to depart. There on the bank he found the prophesied sign: a white sow with thirty white piglets. He sacrificed them all to Juno on her altar.

That night, the Tiber miraculously calmed his current. The river lay still as a quiet pond, with not a ripple to resist the oars. The ships glided upstream as if on glass. Through a full day and night they rowed between green banks. At noon the next day, they spotted distant towers and scattered huts, the modest beginnings of what would one day be Rome. They turned toward shore. It happened to be a sacred festival. King Evander and his son Pallas were sacrificing to Hercules in a grove outside the city walls.

When the Arcadians saw armed ships glittering through the trees, they leaped up in alarm and abandoned the feast. But bold young Pallas snatched a javelin and ran to the riverbank. 'Strangers!' he called. 'Who are you, and what do you want? Do you bring peace or war?' Aeneas stood on the high stern, holding an olive branch. 'We are Trojans,' he said, 'provoked to war by the Latins. We seek King Evander's friendship.' Pallas was struck by the famous name. 'Whatever you need, your fame commands it. Come ashore as a friend and a guest.' He clasped the stranger's hand and led him to the grove.

Aeneas spoke first to the old king: 'Best of Greeks, though I know your ancestry connects you to the very kings who besieged Troy, I come without fear. Our bloodlines share a common source. Dardanus, our Trojan founder, was born of Atlas's daughter Electra. Your ancestor Mercury was born of Atlas's daughter Maia. So Atlas is father to both our lines. I sent no embassy ahead. I came myself, in person, to offer you alliance. The Rutulians who attack us would swallow your small kingdom next. If we fall, nothing will stand between them and dominion over all Italy. Accept our friendship. We have brave hearts and strong arms.'

Evander studied the Trojan's face with wonder. 'How well I remember your father Anchises! When I was a boy, Priam visited our Arcadian court with his brilliant retinue. But Anchises outshone them all. I was awestruck. I sought his friendship eagerly, and when he left, he gave me a Lycian quiver, a Cretan bow, an embroidered cloak, and two golden bridles that my son still uses. The alliance you ask for, I offer as your right. Stay for tonight's festival, and tomorrow I will send you off with supplies and men.' He restored the interrupted feast, seated Aeneas on a lion-skin throne, and they ate and drank together.

When their hunger was satisfied, Evander explained the festival. 'We honor Hercules not from superstition but from gratitude. See that cliff with the ruined cave? The monster Cacus lived there, half beast, half man, a son of Vulcan who breathed smoke and fire. He hung the heads and limbs of his victims on the door. When Hercules came through these lands driving the cattle he had won from three-bodied Geryon, Cacus stole eight of the finest animals and dragged them backward into his cave so their tracks would point the wrong way.'

Evander continued the tale. 'When Hercules prepared to move on, the stolen cattle bellowed from inside the cave, betraying the thief. Hercules flew into a rage and climbed the cliff. Cacus bolted inside and dropped the massive stone door, chained with iron. Hercules circled the mountain three times, tried the entrance three times, and sat down three times in frustration. Then he spotted a jutting pinnacle of flint above the cave. He braced himself and shoved with all his strength until the whole cliff broke free and crashed into the river. The sky cracked open. The cave was exposed to daylight. Cacus cowered below, bellowing and spewing useless smoke. Hercules plunged through the darkness, found the monster, and seized him by the throat. He squeezed until Cacus's eyes burst from their sockets. The doors were torn open. The stolen cattle breathed free air again. From that day, we have honored Hercules at this altar, and so we shall forever. Now fill your cups and praise our common god.'

He crowned his temples with a double wreath of black and white poplar, and all poured wine in honor of Hercules. Evening came. Priests in animal skins led a torchlit procession. A fresh feast was served. Two choirs, one of old men and one of young, sang the labors of Hercules: how as a baby he strangled serpents, how he conquered Troy and Oechalia, endured the labors imposed by Juno and Eurystheus, slew the Centaurs and the Cretan bull and the Nemean lion, made Cerberus cower at the gates of hell, and faced the hundred-headed Hydra of Lerna. When the rites were done, the cheerful company retired.

The old king walked slowly homeward between young Pallas and Aeneas, beguiling the way with tales. Aeneas marveled at everything and asked eagerly about the ancient monuments. Evander said: 'These woods were first home to nymphs and fauns and wild men who knew no laws, no farming, no crafts. They ate what the forest and the hunt provided. Then Saturn came, fleeing his son Jupiter's power. He gathered the scattered savages, gave them laws and customs, and called the land Latium, because here he lay hidden safely. Under his rule, the Golden Age flourished. Later, meaner races came, and kings, and the river that was once called Albula took the name Tiber from a drowned tyrant. I myself arrived last, an exile from Arcadia, led here by my mother's prophecy and heaven's command.'

Walking on, Evander pointed out the altar of Carmenta, his prophetic mother, who had foretold that this place would one day be Rome's imperial seat. He showed the cave of Pan, the Asylum that Romulus would later establish, the Tarpeian Rock, now bare but already touched with superstitious awe. The Arcadians felt some divine presence there, though they could not name the god. They reached Evander's humble court. 'Hercules himself entered through this same door,' said the king, 'and was content with my poor hospitality. Dare to despise wealth, and make yourself worthy of a god.' He led Aeneas inside and gave him a bed of leaves covered with a bearskin. Night fell. Venus, anxious for her son with war approaching, lay beside her husband Vulcan and spoke with all the power of her beauty: 'While Troy was falling, I never asked you for help. But now Aeneas is fated to rule in Italy, and cruel nations are arming against him. A mother begs for her son. You made armor for Thetis's boy and for Aurora's. Now make it for mine.' She wrapped her snowy arms around him. The god melted at her touch, and the old familiar fire ran through his bones.

Vulcan answered: 'You need not beg or doubt my love. If you had asked long ago, I could have armed the Trojans. Nothing that fire and craft can do is beyond my power when love commands.' He gathered her in his arms. Then, while the night was still deep, he rose from bed, as a woman rises early to spin by lamplight, not from pleasure but to keep her children fed.

He flew to his forge: an island between Sicily and Lipari, rising on smoking rocks above caves where Aetna's fires burn. The Cyclopes were hard at work, hammering a thunderbolt for Jupiter. Three prongs of twisted rain, three of fire, three of wind, and three of terrifying flame were mixed together. Others polished Mars's chariot and Athena's serpent-covered shield, renewing the gold on its Gorgon face.

'Set aside all other work,' Vulcan ordered. 'We forge arms for a hero. I need your fullest strength and skill.' Without delay, they heaped the furnace with molten silver, brass, gold, and lethal steel. Seven layers they welded into a single great shield. One pumped the bellows, another quenched the hissing metal. The cave groaned with the rhythm of their hammers, and sparks flew as the tongs turned the glowing mass.

While Vulcan's forge rang on its island, morning came to Evander's humble palace. The old king rose, put on his sandals, strapped on his sword, threw a panther skin over his shoulders, and went with his two guard dogs to meet Aeneas. They sat apart and Evander spoke: 'Great prince, while you survive, Troy is not lost. But my own strength is small. The Tiber hems us in on one side, the Latins press on the other. Yet I can offer you a mighty alliance. Nearby lies the Etruscan city of Caere. Its people suffered unspeakable cruelties under the tyrant Mezentius, who bound the living to the dead until they rotted. At last they revolted, burned his palace, and killed his guards. He fled to Turnus. Now the Tuscans demand his return for punishment. Their army sits on the coast, ready to sail, but an oracle told them they must find a foreign leader. They offered me the command, but I am too old. My son Pallas is half Sabine, not fully foreign. You, Aeneas, fit the prophecy perfectly. Take this command. I give you Pallas, my only son, to learn the art of war at your side, along with two hundred of my best horsemen. Pallas brings two hundred more of his own.'

Scarcely had he spoken when Aeneas and Achates sat in gloomy silence, overwhelmed by the odds they faced. But then Venus sent a sign. Thunder rolled three times across a clear sky. They looked up and saw, shining among the clouds, a flash of divine armor, red as fire, clanging like tempered steel. The others trembled, but Aeneas recognized his mother's promise. 'This sign is mine,' he told the old king. 'My goddess mother foretold that Vulcan would send me arms from heaven. Now Turnus will pay dearly. The Tiber will run red with Rutulian shields and corpses.'

He rose and rekindled the fires on Hercules's altar. Then he and Evander sacrificed together and reviewed the troops. Aeneas selected the bravest for the march to the Tuscan camp. The rest floated downriver to bring news to the Trojan camp. Evander gave Aeneas a fine war-horse draped in a lion's skin with golden claws. Word of the march spread through the little city. Mothers wept and prayed, and the threat of war loomed larger with every moment.

Old Evander embraced his son Pallas and could not let go. Tears streamed down his face. 'If only the gods would give me back my youth, when I killed three-lived Herilus beneath Praeneste's wall! Then neither death nor distance could tear me from my boy. But hear me, Jupiter: if fate preserves my son and I live to see him return, then let me endure any suffering. But if some unspeakable doom awaits him, let me die now, while hope and fear still balance, while I hold him in my arms, before the fatal news can reach me.' He spoke and collapsed. His servants carried him to his bed.
