The horsemen rode out through the open gates. Aeneas led, with Achates at his side and the Trojan captains behind. Young Pallas shone among the Arcadian troop like the morning star rising from the sea, shaking dewdrops from its bright hair, scattering the darkness. The women crowded the walls and towers, watching the dust cloud and the glinting armor until the riders disappeared. They marched across the heath toward the Tuscan camp.

Near a grove sacred to Silvanus, where a stream washed the Tuscan town, Aeneas found the great Etruscan army spread across the plain, led by Tarchon. He brought his Trojans and Arcadians into the camp, refreshed his men, and rested the horses.

Then Venus herself descended through the clouds, bearing the divine arms. She found her son alone by the cool river. Without disguise, she showed him her full heavenly beauty and said: 'Here is Vulcan's finished work, as I promised. Now you need not fear any Rutulian or haughty Turnus.' She embraced him and laid the gleaming armor beneath an oak. Aeneas turned the pieces over in his hands, dazzled with delight. The helmet blazed with fire. The sword was keen, the breastplate burned with gold. The spear was long and sharp. But the shield surpassed them all. On its face, Vulcan had engraved the future history of Rome. There lay the she-wolf in Mars's green cave, nursing the twin founders. Nearby, the rape of the Sabine women and the war that followed, then the peace sealed before Jupiter's altar. He saw the traitor Mettus torn apart by four horses for breaking his oath. He saw Porsenna besieging Rome to restore the tyrant Tarquin, while brave Horatius held the bridge and Cloelia swam the Tiber with the captive girls. Manlius guarded the Capitol, and the silver goose cackled its warning of the Gauls' midnight assault. He saw the Gauls with golden hair and golden torques climbing the walls. He saw the leaping Salii and the dancing Luperci, and the solemn matrons riding to their temples. Below, in Tartarus, Catiline hung on his rock with the Furies hissing around him, while in the fields of the blessed, Cato dispensed his laws.

Between these scenes, a golden sea spread across the shield, its silver waves churned by diving dolphins. There the battle of Actium blazed: Caesar Augustus on the stern, his temples streaming fire, the Julian star above his head, with Agrippa beside him. Opposite stood Antony with his barbarian allies, eastern kings and Arabian troops, and behind him his Egyptian queen with her clash of cymbals. Monster gods of Egypt fought against Neptune, Venus, and Athena. Mars raged in the center. The Furies swooped down. Discord strode through the carnage in her torn and bloody robes. Apollo drew his bow from his Actian cliff, and at the sight the whole East fled. Cleopatra called the winds and ran, pale with the shadow of her approaching death. The Nile opened his arms to receive the fleeing fleet. Then Caesar entered Rome in triple triumph. Three hundred temples were consecrated. The streets rang with song and celebration. He sat before Apollo's marble porch, receiving the tribute of conquered nations who filed past in all their varied dress and languages. The tamed Euphrates and the Rhine bowed their heads. The wild Dahae and the painted Morini, the last of humankind, marched in the procession.

These scenes, wrought by Vulcan's art and brought by Venus's hand, filled the hero with joy and wonder. He did not know the names or the events, but he lifted onto his shoulder the fame and the future of his race.

chapters.title: Book IX
paragraphs: Turnus seizes the chance while Aeneas is away, attacks the Trojan camp, and tries to burn the fleet. The ships are miraculously transformed into sea nymphs. The Trojans, under siege, send Nisus and Euryalus on a daring night mission to reach Aeneas. Their friendship and tragic end provide one of the poem's most admired episodes.

While Aeneas sought allies far away, Juno sent rainbow-winged Iris to Turnus, who sat alone in a sacred grove. 'What no god could grant you,' she said, 'this day provides. Aeneas has left the camp defenseless, gone to beg help from the Arcadians and Tuscans. Strike now, while the moment favors you.' She spoke and flew upward, painting a rainbow across the sky.

Turnus raised his eyes and hands to heaven. 'Iris, what divine power sends you through the parting clouds? I see the sky split open and the stars dancing. I accept these happy omens and follow wherever the god leads.' He scooped water from a stream, tossed it skyward, and loaded the heavens with vows.

The allied army marched across the plain in brilliant order. Messapus led the van. The sons of Tyrrheus brought up the rear. In the center, Turnus towered above the rest, his plumed helmet blazing. They advanced in silence, majestic and slow as the Ganges in flood. From the ramparts, the Trojans saw the dust cloud approaching. Caicus shouted the alarm: 'To arms! Man the walls! The Latins are coming!'

The Trojans shut their gates and lined the battlements, obeying Aeneas's strict orders not to risk battle in open field but to hold their fortifications. Turnus rode up with twenty horsemen. He wore a golden helmet with a crimson crest and sat a piebald Thracian steed. He hurled his lance at the walls as a challenge. Applauding shouts rang out.

Turnus was amazed to find a race that would not come out and fight. Like a hungry wolf circling a sheepfold in the rain, snapping his jaws but unable to reach the lambs safely nursing beneath their mothers, Turnus prowled around the camp, searching every passage for a way in. At last he spotted the fleet, moored beneath the walls where the tide protected it. He snatched a flaming torch and his men armed themselves with fire. Burning brands flew at the ships. Smoke and sparks swirled to the sky. What power, O Muses, could save the Trojan fleet from the flames?

Long ago, when Aeneas first cut timber on Mount Ida, the great goddess Cybele had gone to her son Jupiter: 'Now that you rule heaven, grant me one request. Those pines from my sacred grove, my beloved forest, gave the Trojan prince his ships. Do not let storms or waves destroy them. Let it be their safety that they were once mine.' Jupiter answered: 'Mother, you ask me to override fate? No mortal craft can claim immortality. But I will grant this: when the ships have carried Aeneas safely to Italy, they shall shed their mortal forms and become sea nymphs.' He sealed the vow by the black waters of Styx and shook the heavens with his nod.

Now the fated hour arrived. As Turnus's fires licked the hulls, a dazzling light shot across the sky from the east. Cymbals and flutes sounded from a cloud, and a tremendous voice shook both armies: 'Trojans, do not trouble to defend my ships. Turnus will burn the sea itself before he burns my sacred pines. Go free, my children. Become nymphs of the deep.' At the goddess's command, the ships snapped their mooring ropes, plunged like dolphins beneath the waves, and rose again as beautiful sea maidens, one for every vessel that had been a ship.

The enemy stood amazed. Even the Tiber reared his head in wonder. But Turnus alone was undaunted. He rallied his trembling troops: 'These portents threaten the Trojans, not us. Jupiter has taken away their only means of escape. They cannot flee. Half the world is already lost to them. We hold the land, and thousands of Italian warriors surround their pitiful ditch. I do not fear their fated oracles. It was fated they should reach Italy, and they have. My fate is to destroy them with fire and sword. The Greeks punished them for stealing one wife. Shall we do less? They trust their feeble wall, but Troy had divine walls too, and burned. No wooden horse is needed here. We will attack by daylight. They will learn these are no sleeping Greeks kept at bay for ten years by a boy named Hector. Now rest. Tomorrow will finish this war.'

Messapus was given command of the night watch. Fourteen captains with seven hundred horsemen ringed the camp with fires. The Rutulians feasted, drank, and gambled through the night, their campfires burning bright.

The Trojans watched from the ramparts. They reinforced the walls, connected the towers with bridges, and stationed guards at every point. Mnestheus and Sergestus shared command, as Aeneas had instructed. The soldiers drew lots for their watches.

Near the gate, Nisus stood his turn on guard. His father was Hyrtacus, his mother a huntress. He was deadly with the javelin and even deadlier with the bow. Beside him was Euryalus, the most beautiful youth in the Trojan army, his cheeks just showing the first soft down of manhood. Their friendship was their deepest bond, and tonight they shared the same post.

Nisus whispered: 'Is it the gods who put this fire in me, or does desire itself become our god? I cannot rest. Look at the enemy camp. Their fires are guttering out. Most of them lie drunk and senseless. I can see a way through to Aeneas's position. If the council will send you after me, I will cut a path through those sleepers. Fame enough for me.'

Euryalus's eyes blazed with eagerness. 'You would go alone and leave me behind? My father trained me in arms from the cradle. I was born in a siege. Do you think I value this life so highly I would not spend it to win glory? Send me with you.'

Nisus begged him to stay behind. 'If something goes wrong, and in war a thousand things can, your young life is worth more than mine. I need someone to mourn me and, if possible, buy back my body for burial. Do not bring this grief on your mother, who followed you here when every other woman stayed in Sicily.' But Euryalus would not be moved: 'You argue in vain. No more delays.' They woke the relief guards and went together to the council tent.

The Trojan captains sat in worried conference, leaning on their spears, debating how to send word to Aeneas. Nisus and Euryalus begged admission and were brought before young Ascanius. Nisus spoke: 'Fathers, do not judge us by our years. The enemy lies drunk and careless. We know a path along the shore to Evander's city. Give us leave, and you will see Aeneas return with Tuscan allies before another day is done.'

Old Alethes wept with joy: 'Our country's gods have not abandoned us, while such brave youth remains.' He embraced them both. 'The greatest reward the gods and your own valor will give you. The rest, our general will bestow, and young Ascanius will owe you all his life.'

Ascanius spoke: 'I swear by our household gods and by old Vesta's sacred flame, my whole fortune rests on bringing my father back. If you succeed, Nisus, I give you two silver goblets from conquered Arisba, two tripods, two gold talents, and Dido's precious cup. If we conquer Italy, you shall have Turnus's horse, his armor, his shield, and his plumed helmet. Twelve captive men, twelve handmaids, and a great estate of Latinus's land. And you, Euryalus, whose age is closest to mine, I claim you for my heart's brother. One faith, one fame, one fate shall bind us.'

Euryalus answered: 'Time will never find me unworthy of this brave beginning. But grant me one thing, or all rewards are vain. My mother, of Priam's royal blood, followed me here when every other woman stayed behind. I leave her now without a farewell kiss, without a word. I could not bear to say goodbye. Be a son to her when I am gone. Support her in her old age. Let me take that hope with me, and I can face anything.' The whole council wept.

Ascanius was most deeply moved. 'Your mother shall be mine,' he said, 'wanting nothing but the name of Creusa. Whatever comes of your brave mission, I swear by my father's oath: the rewards I promised you shall be hers if you do not return.'
Weeping as he spoke, he unbuckled his golden sword, the work of Lycaon, in an ivory sheath, and gave it to Euryalus. Mnestheus gave a lion's hide, and Alethes his own battle-proven helmet.

Armed and ready, the two friends set out through the gate. The noble Trojans followed them with prayers and vows. Young Ascanius, wise beyond his years, sent messages for his father. But the winds scattered every word.

They crossed the trenches and entered the enemy camp. Bodies sprawled everywhere, drunk and snoring. Chariots stood unhitched along the shore, weapons and wine cups tangled together. Nisus whispered: 'Now is our chance. Keep watch while I cut a path.' He drew his sword and fell on sleeping Rhamnes, a king and prophet beloved by Turnus, but prophecy could not save him from fate. Nisus killed his slaves, then moved to Remus and his retinue: the armor-bearer, the charioteer between the horses, and Remus himself, whose head flew from his neck in a fountain of blood. He killed Lamyrus, Lamus, and young Serranus, who had fallen asleep after a night of dice and drinking. He was like a starving lion loose in a sheepfold, tearing the silent flock while they trembled beneath his jaws.

Euryalus matched his fury. He killed Fadus, Hebesus, and Rhoetus, who woke just in time to see the sword that killed him. The blade pierced him through a wine jar where he crouched, and blood and wine poured out together.

They reached Messapus's lines, where the fires were dying. Nisus saw danger in the growing light. 'Enough. Dawn is coming. We have cut a wide road through the slaughtered. Let us go.' Euryalus reluctantly agreed, but he could not resist the glittering spoils. He took Rhamnes' horse-blanket and strapped on a magnificent gold-studded belt. Then, fatally, he put on Messapus's gleaming helmet with its tall crest. They left the camp and took the road.

But three hundred Volscian horsemen, led by Volcens, were riding that very road with dispatches for Turnus. In the fading moonlight, the borrowed helmet caught the light and betrayed Euryalus. 'Halt!' Volcens shouted. 'Who goes there?' The two friends said nothing and sprinted for the woods. The horsemen fanned out to block every path. The forest was thick with beech and fern, almost impenetrable. Euryalus, burdened with spoils and blinded by fear, lost his way among the tangled paths. Nisus found his way through and emerged on the far side. Only then did he realize his friend was not behind him. 'Where have I left him?' he cried, and plunged back into the dark forest.

He heard the trampling of horses and the shouts of men. He saw Euryalus surrounded, dragged struggling from the undergrowth. What could he do? Rush in and die with him, or try to save him with a throw? He looked up at the moon: 'Diana, goddess of the night, guide my spear.' He hurled it from the darkness. It flew hissing through the air and struck Sulmo in the back, piercing his armor and lodging in his heart. Sulmo staggered and fell. A second javelin sang through Tagus's temples and buried itself in his brain. Volcens looked wildly for the hidden thrower but could not find him. 'Then you will pay for both!' he screamed, and charged at Euryalus with drawn sword. Nisus could not bear it. He burst from hiding and screamed: 'Me! Turn your swords on me! The fault is mine. He could not have harmed you. His only crime was loving his friend too much.' But it was too late. The sword had already driven through the boy's tender side. Euryalus fell. The blood gushed from the wound and stained the ground. His beautiful head drooped on his breast like a white poppy sinking under rain. Maddened with grief and rage, Nisus charged into the packed horsemen, seeking only Volcens. Hemmed in on every side, he fought through and found him. As he died on a dozen swords, his own blade drove through Volcens's mouth and out the back of his throat. Then Nisus fell across his dead friend's body, and at last found rest.
O fortunate pair! If my verses have any power, your fame will live as long as Rome endures and the Roman eagle flies.

At dawn, the Rutulians found the carnage and carried the dead to camp. They recognized Messapus's stolen helmet. Turnus armed for battle and raised the severed heads of Nisus and Euryalus on spears for the Trojans to see.

The Trojans manned their walls. Looking out, they saw the heads of their friends, still recognizable despite the gore. The terrible news flew through the camp and reached Euryalus's mother. The blood drained from her face, the shuttle fell from her hands. She ran screaming to the ramparts. 'Is this how you look, my son? You who were all my comfort in old age? How could you go without a word to your own mother? Now you lie on foreign ground, torn by dogs and vultures. I never dressed your body for burial or closed your eyes. This cloth I wove for you day and night will never wrap your limbs. Where shall I follow? If there is any pity left in war, strike me down, Rutulians. Or let Jupiter hurl his bolt and end my misery.' Her cries shook the army's courage. Ilioneus and weeping Ascanius ordered her carried gently inside.

The trumpet sounded and the Rutulians advanced with a roar. They formed a tortoise of shields and pressed toward the walls. Some raised scaling ladders. Others sought weak points. The Trojans answered with stones and sharpened stakes. Turnus hurled a firebrand at a wooden tower, and the flames caught. The defenders tried to retreat, but the tower collapsed under them. Two were killed in the fall. The rest tumbled down in a tangle of arms and rubble, pierced by their own broken stakes.
Messapus killed Ericetes, and Turnus brought down Helenor, who fought like a cornered boar, knowing escape was hopeless.
Lycus tried to scale the wall and reach his friends' hands above, but Turnus cut him down. 'Did you think you could escape me?' he laughed, and ripped the body from the battlements.

From the towers, the Trojans rained arrows and missiles. Emathion hurled stones, Caeneus wielded the fire-pots. Pandarus and Bitias, huge twin brothers who had been reared in Jupiter's groves on Mount Ida, dared what no one else would: they threw open their gate and stood on either side, armed and defiant, inviting the enemy in.

The Trojans hurled back stones and stakes from the ramparts. Serestus and Mnestheus directed the defense, stationing archers at the towers and spearmen at the gates. Every hand that could lift a weapon was put to work. Even those wounded in earlier fighting returned to the walls.

The Rutulians who charged in were cut to pieces. A vicious fight erupted at the gate. Pandarus and Bitias, like two oak trees on a riverbank, stood their ground. Others joined them on the ramparts, raining javelins down. But Turnus was fighting elsewhere. The Fury Alecto guided Turnus to the open gate. He saw the twins and drove toward them. His spear struck Bitias through his shield, through his double-layered mail, and into his massive chest. The giant crashed to the ground like a pillar toppling from Baiae's harbor into the sea.

When Pandarus saw his brother fall, he heaved the gate shut with his own shoulders. But in his haste, he locked Turnus inside the walls with him and a handful of enemy soldiers. If Turnus had thought to open the gate for his army, the war would have ended that day. But bloodlust and rage drove him only to kill.

Pandarus called out: 'This is not Amata's palace, Turnus. You are trapped inside Trojan walls with no escape.' Turnus smiled coolly: 'Then begin, if you dare. Tell Priam's shade you found another Achilles here.' Pandarus hurled his massive spear, but Juno deflected it. Turnus's sword answered. He split Pandarus from crown to chin with a single stroke, and the giant's two halves fell apart.

Terror seized the Trojans. If Turnus had opened the gate then, the war would have ended. But his fury drove him only toward more slaughter. He killed Phaleris with a javelin through the throat, and Gyges, whose severed arm still clutched its shield. Halys fell, then Phegeus. Others died at the ramparts, not knowing the killer was among them. Turnus was like a blood-drenched lion among a flock.

At last Mnestheus shouted: 'Where are you running? What other walls do you have? One man, trapped inside your own camp, is slaughtering you all and you do nothing?' Shamed, the Trojans rallied and pushed Turnus back step by step toward the river side of the camp.

Turnus killed Ericetes as he climbed the wall and dragged his body down by the heels. Lycus tried to scale the defenses by stealth, reaching upward for his comrades' hands, but Turnus spotted him and pulled him down, tearing away a section of wall with him. The defenders above wept but could not help.

Turnus fought on, retreating slowly. The Trojans pressed him with a forest of spears. He was like a lion beaten back by a ring of hunters: too proud to flee, unable to break through. Three times he charged. Three times the Trojans drove him back.

Still he fought. His helmet rang with stones and arrows. His crest was beaten flat. His shield could barely hold. Mnestheus hurled a javelin that pierced the mail and grazed his side. Drenched in sweat and blood, barely breathing, Turnus gave ground to the river. He leaped, armor and all, into the Tiber. The yellow current received him gently, washed away the blood, and carried him back to his cheering friends.

Nisus and Euryalus were dead. Pandarus and Bitias were dead. The Trojan walls still held, and Turnus had been driven out. But the war was far from over. Both sides counted their losses as the sun set on a day of carnage. Neither army slept easily that night.

Turnus scrambled up the far bank, dripping with river water but burning with shame and fury. His men cheered his return, but the sting of having been driven from the enemy camp by a handful of defenders seared his pride.

The night was restless on both sides. The Trojans strengthened their walls and mourned their dead. The Rutulians nursed their wounded and sharpened their weapons. Both camps knew that worse was yet to come. Somewhere in the darkness, Aeneas was sailing back with Tuscan allies. Time was running out.

Meanwhile the gods looked down. Some favored Troy, some favored Turnus. None could change the thread of fate that drew both peoples toward the bloody fields where the future of Italy would be decided.

As the sun reached its peak, the fighting only intensified. The Rutulians brought up battering rams and siege towers. The Trojans countered with boiling oil and firebrands dropped from above. The air was thick with smoke and screaming. Both sides fought with a fury that left no room for mercy or retreat.

Dawn came, painting the sky with rose. The Trojans lined their walls. The Rutulians formed ranks on the plain. Neither side moved first. The silence before battle settled over the field like a held breath.

Then Turnus raised his great spear and hurled it at the walls. The war cry went up from ten thousand throats. The final phase of the siege had begun. Stones, arrows, and javelins darkened the air. Heroes fell on both sides. The Trojans held their ground, remembering Aeneas's command: hold the walls until I return.

And in the distance, unseen by either army, the Trojan fleet was already rounding the headland, laden with Etruscan warriors. Aeneas stood at the prow, his new shield blazing in the morning light. The war would soon take a very different turn.

But for now, the defenders fought alone. Every hand that could hold a weapon was on the wall. Women carried stones. Boys fetched arrows. The camp that had seemed so feeble held against everything Turnus could throw at it.

Turnus raged below the walls like a storm that cannot break through a mountain. He killed and killed, but the walls would not fall. The Trojans fought with the desperate valor of men who have no retreat. Behind them lay only the river and ruin. Before them stood the pride of Italy.
The day wore on in blood and dust. Neither side gained ground. The dead piled against the base of the walls. The living stepped over them and fought on. It was the longest day any of them had known.

As the sun began its descent, both armies drew apart by unspoken agreement. The Rutulians pulled back to their fires. The Trojans sagged against their battered walls. Somewhere across the water, Aeneas was coming. The Trojans prayed for morning.

chapters.title: Book X
paragraphs: Jupiter calls a council of the gods and forbids them to take sides in the war. Aeneas returns with his Tuscan allies, and a fierce battle follows. Turnus kills young Pallas. Aeneas, burning for revenge, slaughters Lausus and his father Mezentius. The noble death of the pious son and his godless father provides the book's most powerful episode.

The gates of heaven swung open. Jupiter summoned all the gods to his golden palace. From his throne he surveyed the earth below, where the Latin and Trojan camps faced each other. He addressed the assembly.

"Gods of heaven, why have you broken my command and stirred up war between these peoples? The time for battle will come soon enough, when Carthage one day pours through the Alps to attack Rome. Today, let there be peace. Cease interfering and let fate take its course."

Venus spoke first, with passionate indignation: "Father, while Trojans suffer under Italian swords, to whom can I turn if not to you? Turnus rages unchecked. Diomedes, who once wounded me, is asked to join the slaughter. Is this the Italy you promised, the kingdom you swore?"

Juno's heart swelled with rage. "Must I defend myself for protecting what is mine? The Trojans invaded Italy, not the other way around. Paris started the first war. I did not make them sail here. If they will cross the sea and fight for other men's kingdoms, let them face the consequences."
The gods murmured, divided in their sympathies, like wind moaning through the forest before a storm breaks.

Jupiter silenced them all. "Since you cannot agree, I will make no distinction between Trojan and Rutulian. Whatever fortune each man earns today, let him keep it. Jupiter is king of all and favors none. Fate will find its way." He swore by the Styx and shook all Olympus with his nod. The council ended. The gods rose from their golden seats and escorted the Father to his door.
Meanwhile, at the Trojan camp, the Rutulians pressed the siege from every side. The defenders manned their walls, few against many, with no hope of flight and no strength to break out.
The Trojans wished desperately for their absent chief. They were like trapped animals, surrounded by hunters on every side.

Young Ascanius fought among the men, beautiful and bright as a jewel set in gold. He shot his arrows from the ramparts and killed the boasting Numanus, who had taunted the Trojans as weaklings. Apollo himself appeared and praised the boy but warned him to fight no more that day.
Nor was Ismarus lacking in the battle, sending arrows from afar, nor the sons of Imbrasides, who fought with spear and fire.
While mortal war raged on Italian soil, Aeneas was cutting through the night sea, heading home with his Tuscan allies. He had sealed his alliance with Tarchon, and the fleet was racing for the Tiber.
They set sail with favorable winds. Aeneas stood at the prow. The sea-nymphs that had once been his ships recognized their master and swam alongside, leaping through the waves.
Now, sacred Muses, tell me who these Tuscan warriors were, what ships they sailed, and what armies they led.
Brave Massicus commanded a thousand men in the Tiger. Abas brought six hundred archers in his painted ship. Astur of Caere, handsome and proud of his horses, led three hundred.
Astur followed in the watery field, proud of his well-trained horse and his painted shield. Three hundred more followed from Caere, Minio, old Pyrgi, and unhealthy Graviscae.
Cinyras too deserves to be named, and brave Cupavo, whose helmet bore swan feathers in memory of his father Cycnus, transformed by grief for Phaethon into a white bird.
Ocnus led his native band from Mantua, the city his mother the prophetess Manto founded. His army wore blue plumes on their helmets.
Five hundred more came, armed with hatred of Mezentius, carried on ships adorned with the image of old Mincius, son of Lake Benacus.
Thirty ships in all brought these warriors across the shining sea for Troy's relief.
Night had fallen. Aeneas sat at the tiller, steering through the dark water, unable to sleep.
He prayed to the goddess Cybele: "Mother of the gods, protect my men and bless our voyage. Let tomorrow bring us victory."

He spoke, and dawn broke. The shadows fled. He ordered his men to take up their shields and raise the standards. Standing on the high stern, he held aloft the blazing shield that Vulcan had made. The Trojans on the distant walls saw it flash like a comet and raised a mighty shout.

Turnus was amazed to see the fleet approaching, its shields glittering. But he was not afraid. "Now they come to us by sea. I will meet them at the waterline and slaughter them as they land. We need no wooden horse here."
He deployed his forces along the beach, some to block the landing, others to hold the river crossings.

The Trojans beached their ships wherever they could. Some leaped from the prows into the shallows. Others crossed on makeshift bridges. Tarchon drove his galley straight onto the sand, but the keel cracked on a hidden reef and his men spilled into the surf, tangled with oars and wreckage.
Aeneas shouted to his Tuscans: "Now is the hour! Follow me! Break through to the shore!" His men pulled with desperate fury, drove their ships grinding up the beach, and leaped armed into the waves.
Turnus saw the landing and charged. Both sides collided at the waterline.
Aeneas called for more spears and hurled them with deadly aim. He killed Theron and Lichas and Cisseus and Gyas, despite their powerful arms.
The Sabine Clausus struck down Dryops, and Sacrator killed Hydaspes. The fighting was fierce and confused, like the clash of opposing winds over a heaving sea.
But in another part of the field, the Arcadian horsemen fared badly against the Latin cavalry. Unaccustomed to fighting on foot in rough terrain, they had dismounted and were being pushed back.

Young Pallas saw them retreating and rallied them with shame and anger. "Where are you running? By your king, by your honor, follow me!" He charged into the enemy, killing Lagus with a javelin through the spine, then Hisbo, then Sthenius and Anchemolus.
Halesus came on fiercely, and Lausus, no small part of the war, held the Rutulian line together.
But Lausus and Pallas were kept apart by fate, for each was reserved for a greater opponent.
Turnus's sister Juturna warned him that Pallas was wreaking havoc. Turnus drove his chariot through the press and shouted: "Stand back, all of you. Pallas is mine alone."

Pallas faced him without fear, though the gap in their strength was vast. He prayed to Hercules: "By my father's hospitality, by the table where you feasted, help me strip this boaster of his armor and let him die seeing his conqueror." Hercules heard and wept, but Jupiter said: "Each man's day is fixed. The brave can only make it glorious."

Pallas threw his spear. It pierced the edge of Turnus's shield and grazed his shoulder. Turnus balanced his great shaft and said: "See if mine strikes deeper." It drove through Pallas's shield, through his breastplate, and into his chest. The boy pulled the weapon out, but his blood and his life came with it. He fell, and his armor clanged against the earth.

Turnus stood over the body. "Arcadians, carry this message to Evander: I send him back his Pallas as he deserved. Whatever honor a tomb can give, I freely grant. But his welcome to Aeneas will cost him dearly." He pressed his foot on the corpse and stripped away the heavy gold belt with its engraved scene of murder.
Turnus did not know what he took. The spoils of Pallas would bring him ruin. There are times when the gods let men seize what will destroy them.
The Arcadians carried the body back on a shield. Pallas, the source of his father's joy and grief, returned a lifeless trophy. One day had given him his first battle and taken his last.

When the news reached Aeneas, his blood turned to ice, then to fire. He cut a path of slaughter toward Turnus. He took eight young men alive, to sacrifice at Pallas's funeral. He captured Magus, who begged for mercy by Anchises' shade. Aeneas refused: "The shade of Pallas demands this." He drove his sword through the man's throat.
Apollo's priest Haemonides stood in the prince's path, his sacred robes gleaming. Aeneas killed him and left his body for the birds. He killed Tarquitus and left his severed limbs unburied.
Vulcanian Caeculus and Umbro from the hills rallied against him but could not stand. Aeneas was unstoppable.
He killed Lycas and Antaeus, two of Turnus's captains, and Numa, and Camers the nobleman whose father was Volcens.

Lucagus and Liger charged in their chariot. Aeneas hurled a spear through the shield and into Lucagus's groin. As he fell, Liger begged for his life. "Trojans do not beg," Aeneas replied, and ran him through.
He raged across the field like a storm or a flood, scattering everything before him. At last Ascanius and the Trojans broke out of their camp and joined the battle.
Jupiter spoke to Juno: "The war has run long enough. What is your will?"

Juno answered: "If you will allow me, I can save Turnus from death today. He is fated to die, I know. But let me delay it a little while." Jupiter agreed: "If it is only a postponement, take him. But do not change the outcome of the war."

Juno formed a phantom of Aeneas from mist and shadow, gave it false armor and a false voice. It strode before Turnus, taunting him. Turnus chased it. The phantom ran toward a ship moored at the dock and leaped aboard. Turnus followed.
The moment his feet touched the deck, Juno snapped the mooring rope. The ship carried Turnus far out to sea. The phantom dissolved into thin air.

Turnus stood on the drifting ship, stunned and enraged. He raised his hands to heaven: "Jupiter, what have I done to deserve this shame? Where am I going? How can I face my men? I left them dying while I chased a ghost." He considered throwing himself on his own sword or swimming back to shore. Three times he tried each and three times Juno held him back. At last the current carried him to the coast of his father's kingdom, and he waded ashore in disgrace.
With Turnus gone, Mezentius took his place, burning with fresh fury. The Tuscan veterans, who hated him above all men, concentrated their attack. But Mezentius stood like a cliff against the waves.
Haughty Hebrus fell dead at his feet. Then Latagus, killed by a boulder hurled at his face. Then Palmus, hamstrung as he ran.
Like a savage boar hunted down from the mountains, Mezentius bristled with spears and held his ground, snarling at the ring of enemies.

Acron came charging, a man who had left his bride and his unfinished wedding to join the war. Mezentius speared him through. Orodes turned and ran but got a spear in the back. Standing over him, Mezentius said: "You were no small part of this war, but here you lie."
Caedicus killed Alcathous. Sacrator killed Hydaspes. The Rutulians rallied behind Mezentius's example.
Equal deaths fell on both sides. They advanced and retreated in turn, and the gods watched as mortal fates swung in the balance.
Once more Mezentius charged. Aeneas marked him and stood ready.
Aeneas threw his javelin. It pierced the shield, broke through the triple plates, and lodged in Mezentius's hip. Aeneas drew his sword and charged. But young Lausus threw himself between them.
The sight of his father's blood fired Lausus to reckless courage. He ran in and caught Aeneas's sword on his shield, giving Mezentius time to stagger back.

Like a farmer sheltering from a hailstorm, Aeneas waited behind his shield while Lausus's companions hurled their javelins. Then he shouted: "Stop! Your love for your father is leading you to a death beyond your strength." But Lausus only pressed closer.

Aeneas drove his sword through the boy's shield, through his tunic, through his chest. The blade drank his blood and his life. When the prince saw the young man's face, pale and already fading, he groaned. He reached out and lifted the body. "What can I give you, brave boy, worthy of your great heart? Keep the arms you loved. I send you to your father's shade." He called the attendants and raised the body himself, so the blood would not stain those beautiful curls.

Meanwhile Mezentius stood by the Tiber, washing his wound. His helmet hung from a branch. His armor weighed him down. He called for Lausus again and again. Then the messengers came, carrying the body on a shield, killed by Aeneas's hand.

The old man's white hair was matted with dust. He raised his hands to heaven, then clutched the corpse. "My son, was I so hungry for life that I let you take my place? Now I know the depth of my exile and the bitterness of my wound. I stained your name with my sins. Driven from the throne, I owed this punishment to my people's hatred. I should have given my life a hundred times. But I live still, and I have not yet left the light." He hauled himself to his feet and called for his war-horse Rhaebus.

He mounted despite his wound and spoke to the horse: "We have lived long enough, old friend. Today you will bring back Aeneas's head and his spoils, and share my revenge for Lausus. Or else we die together. You have never served an unworthy master." The horse bore him back to the battlefield.

He shouted to Aeneas: "Boast all you want. You killed my son. That was the only wound that could reach me. I came here to die, not to plead. But first, take this." He hurled a javelin that glanced off the shield, then another that struck a bystander dead. He rode in circles, launching spear after spear, but the divine shield held them all.
Aeneas ran out of patience. He hurled his own spear. It struck Rhaebus between the temples. The great horse reared and threw Mezentius, then crashed down on top of him.

Pinned beneath his dying horse, Mezentius looked up at the Trojan standing over him. "Why should I beg for my life? I came here to die. My son and I made no truce with you. I ask one thing only: let my body rest in the same earth as Lausus. I know my people hate me. Protect my corpse from their fury." He said this, then opened his throat to the descending blade, and the blood poured out over his armor.

chapters.title: Book XI
paragraphs: Aeneas erects a trophy from Mezentius's spoils, grants a truce for burying the dead, and sends Pallas's body home with great ceremony. Latinus calls a council to propose peace, which causes bitter argument between Turnus and Drances. Meanwhile, a cavalry battle rages in which the warrior maiden Camilla fights brilliantly until she is treacherously killed. The Latins are routed.

Scarce had the rosy morning risen above the waves when Aeneas, though eager to bury his dead and shaken by the losses of war, stood upon a mound and raised a trophy. He stripped Mezentius's armor and hung it on an oak: the bloody crest, the shattered spears, the pierced breastplate. His captains gathered around him.

"The greatest part of our work is done," he told them. "Here hangs Mezentius, the first fruits of the tyrant-king. Now our road leads to Latinus and his walls. Prepare your arms, sharpen your spirits. Let no man be caught unprepared when the gods give the signal to march."
Then he turned to a sadder duty. He went to where Pallas lay. Old Acoetes, who had once been Pallas's tutor and guardian, knelt beside the body, weeping.

Aeneas mourned over the corpse. "Unlucky boy, Fortune gave you to me and then snatched you away. You will never see my kingdom in Italy or ride home in triumph to your father. This is not what I promised Evander when he embraced me and sent you to learn the hardships of war. Even now he may be praying for your safe return. And we can only send him a body."
Acoetes attended the funeral bier, supported by his friends, barely able to walk. A long procession of Trojans followed, weeping.
Then envoys arrived from Latinus under a flag of truce, begging for permission to bury their dead. Aeneas granted it readily.
He went further: "I came not to make war on the Latins but to find a home. This quarrel is Turnus's doing. Let Turnus settle it in single combat. That would have been better for everyone."

The ambassadors were struck by his fairness. Old Drances, who already hated Turnus, answered: "Great prince, your fame matches your fortune. How can we repay such generosity? Let us make peace between your people and ours. Let Turnus build his own walls, if he dares. We will help the Trojans raise theirs." All agreed, and a twelve-day truce was sworn.
Trojans and Latins worked side by side, felling trees for the funeral pyres. The hills rang with axes.

The news of Pallas's death reached Evander's small city on the Tiber. The Arcadians who had lined the banks with festive torches now carried only funeral brands. The procession stretched along the road. When the bier arrived, Evander threw himself on the body.

"O Pallas," he cried, "you broke your promise to me. I begged you to fight with caution. But the sweetness of your first battle carried you away. At least you did not die dishonorably. At least I do not have to blush for my son. But I would give back all the Tuscan alliance, all the heaps of Italian dead, to have you standing here alive. I am not ashamed of my tears. Aeneas, I do not blame you. My only prayer now is this: let Turnus pay. Keep Turnus alive until your sword can avenge my son. That is all I ask of life."
The next morning restored the world to work. Aeneas and Tarchon built a great pyre on the beach. The funeral rites for the Trojan dead were performed with full military honors.

The Latins did the same across the plain. Some bodies were burned where they lay. Others were carted home for burial in the city. The rest went up in a vast unnamed bonfire. The fields blazed with so many pyres that the countryside was lit for three days.

On the third day, they raked the ashes, gathered the bones, and heaped earth over them. In Latinus's city, the grief was sharpest. Mothers and widows and orphans cursed the war and cursed Turnus. "Let him settle it himself," they cried, "since he claims the crown and the glory."
Inside the palace, the scene was more solemn and more bitter. The dead of noble houses were mourned, and angry voices blamed Turnus for everything.

The ambassadors returned from Diomedes with a crushing answer. The great Greek hero, settled in his own Italian city, wanted no more war with Trojans. He had suffered enough from their gods. He advised the Latins to make peace.
Latinus, weighed down with sorrow, finally saw what the gods had been telling him all along. Aeneas was the foreign prince of destiny. Resistance was futile. He called a council.
Venulus delivered Diomedes's answer. A shocked murmur ran through the court. Even the warriors who had hungered for battle sat in uneasy silence.
The murmur grew louder. The factions split. Some demanded immediate peace. Others refused to surrender.

Then the old king spoke from his throne: "I wish we had settled this earlier. It is foolish to debate when the enemy is at the gates. We have been beaten. Our allies refuse us. We are fighting fate. I propose that we cede a strip of territory to the Trojans. Let them build their city, or if they prefer, let them sail for other shores. In either case, let us end this ruinous war."

Drances, who hated Turnus, seized the moment: "We all know the truth, king, but we are afraid to speak it. One man's pride has cost us this disaster. Let him give up his claim to Lavinia. Let him stand aside. Or better yet, let him prove his courage in single combat with Aeneas, instead of feeding the rest of us to death."

Turnus blazed with fury: "You always have plenty of words, Drances, when others do the fighting. But the senate rings with your eloquence while braver men die in the dust. Go ahead, call me a coward. My right hand is piled with the bodies of Trojans I have killed. Can you say the same? But if they want single combat, I will not refuse. Let Aeneas challenge me and I will meet him."

"Now hear my battle plan," Turnus continued. "We are not so weak as Drances pretends. Our allies still outnumber the enemy. Camilla and the Volscians will meet their cavalry. I will set an ambush in the mountain pass where Aeneas must march."
But even as they debated, scouts brought word that Aeneas had broken camp and was marching on the city.
Turnus cut the debate short. "Talk all you want, senators, while the enemy knocks on our gates. I go to fight." He stormed out, shouting orders. Every street filled with rushing soldiers.
The women and old men ran to the walls. Mothers carried their children to the temples and prayed.
Some dug trenches and sharpened stakes. Others piled stones on the battlements. The trumpet called every able-bodied man to arms.

Turnus put on his golden armor, laced the steel across his chest, and strapped on his great sword. He blazed with martial fire, like a stallion that has broken free and charges across the fields toward the mares.

At the city gates, Camilla met him with her Volscian cavalry. She swung down from her horse and said: "If courage may speak, let me take my riders against the Trojan horse. You hide in the mountain pass and guard the road. I will handle the open field."
Turnus looked at the fierce maiden with admiration: "You are Italy's glory. We will share the danger. Take the cavalry and ride out against the Tuscan horsemen. I will spring the ambush."
In a winding valley shut in by hills and dense forest, Turnus set his trap. He hid his men among the trees above a narrow track.

But Diana, watching from heaven, grieved for her beloved Camilla. She told the nymph Opis: "That brave girl is riding to her death. She has been my favorite since childhood, when her father Metabus, fleeing his enemies, strapped her to a javelin and hurled her across a flooding river, vowing her to Diana. I raised her in the wild forests. Now fate sends her to a war she cannot win. Go down and watch. If any man harms her, he will pay with his life."

The raging flood blocked Metabus's escape. He could not swim with the infant. He bound her to his spear, prayed to Diana, and hurled. The javelin sailed across. He plunged in after it and reached the far bank safely. From that day, Camilla lived wild in the forests, a huntress consecrated to Diana.
Opis took her quiver and bow and flew down to the battlefield.

The Trojans and Tuscans advanced together on horseback. When they came within javelin range, both lines charged. Horses screamed and crashed together. Riders hurled their lances, and dust rose so thick it blocked the sun.

The cavalry clashed again with renewed savagery. Horses reared and bit each other. Riders grappled at close range with short swords while their mounts wheeled and stamped. The field was churned to mud. Fallen horses screamed. Riderless mounts galloped through both lines, spreading confusion.

Twice the Tuscans drove the Latins back. Twice the Latins rallied and charged in turn. On the third clash, both sides locked together in close combat. Dying horses rolled on their riders. The ground ran slippery with blood.

Camilla rode through the carnage like a storm. Her bare breast exposed, she fought with javelin, axe, and bow without pause. Wherever she charged, men fell or fled. Her warrior women, Larina, Tulla, and Tarpeia, followed her like a whirlwind.

Who did she kill first, who last? She drove her spear through Euneus's chest. Liris and Pagasus fell to her axe. She unhorsed Amastrus and Tereus, Harpalycus and Demophoon and Chromis. Every arrow she loosed found a mark.
Aunus, a Ligurian trickster, tried to flee. Camilla chased him down and killed him like a hawk catching a dove high above the clouds.

Jupiter himself stirred Tarchon to rally the Tuscans. The great captain shamed his men into fighting and grabbed the enemy warrior Venulus right off his horse, carrying him away like an eagle with a snake.
But the treacherous Arruns had been stalking Camilla, circling at a distance, waiting for his moment. Every time she charged, he followed in her wake, looking for an opening.

When Camilla spotted a Trojan priest in magnificent golden armor and, consumed with desire for the spoils, chased him single-mindedly across the field, Arruns seized his chance. He prayed to Apollo, launched his javelin, and struck her beneath the exposed breast.
The spear stuck fast. Her companions caught her as she swayed. Camilla tried to pull out the weapon but the iron head was lodged between her ribs. She felt the cold blood draining from her limbs.

She called her most faithful companion, Acca. "I have fought my last fight, sister. My vision darkens. Tell Turnus to come at once and hold the city. Farewell." She let go of the reins, slid slowly from her horse, and lay cold on the earth. Her spirit fled with an angry hiss to the shades below.
A roar went up that struck the stars. The Volscians charged with desperate fury, but without their leader they broke apart. The Trojans and Tuscans pressed their advantage.
Diana's nymph Opis watched from a hilltop as Arruns tried to slink away. She fitted an arrow and drew the silver bow.

"You violated Diana's handmaiden," she said. "You will carry no glory home from this." The arrow hissed through the air and struck Arruns dead. His companions did not even notice. His body lay in the dust while Opis flew back to Olympus.

Without Camilla, the Volscians broke and ran. The Rutulians ran. The allies scattered. The Trojans pursued them to the very walls of the city. Women on the towers armed themselves with stakes and firebrands.

The fleeing Latins and the pursuing Trojans jammed together at the gates. Mothers watched their own sons trampled. Some tried to shut the gates, but the press of bodies was too great. Soldiers fell in the ditches and were impaled on stakes. Arrows rained from the walls on friend and foe alike. The dust and the screaming were indescribable.

When the news of Camilla's death and the rout reached Turnus in his mountain ambush, he abandoned his position and marched for the city. Aeneas, no longer blocked, marched through the empty pass. Both armies converged on the plain before Latinus's walls. If night had not fallen, the final battle would have been fought that day. Instead, both sides camped in sight of the city, and the last night of the war began.

chapters.title: Book XII
paragraphs: Turnus challenges Aeneas to single combat. Terms are agreed, but the Rutulians break the truce and wound Aeneas. He is miraculously healed by Venus. He storms the city. The two champions meet at last. Aeneas kills Turnus, and the poem ends.

When Turnus saw the Latins broken and routed, their courage gone and every eye turned on him to fulfill his promise, his fury blazed higher than ever. Like a wounded lion in Africa that welcomes the hunters' spears and shakes the arrow from its mane, Turnus raged and would not be stopped.
He went to the king and spoke with flashing eyes: "No more delay. I challenged Aeneas and I will fight him. Let the coward Drances watch from the walls. Prepare the ground for combat."

He burned with fiercer energy. He called for his horses, the famous Thracian pair that Orithyia gave to Pilumnus, whiter than snow and swifter than the wind. The charioteers clapped their shoulders and combed their manes. Turnus strapped on his breastplate of gold and bronze scales, buckled his sword and shield, and snatched up his great spear.

Latinus tried to dissuade him: "Your courage is proven. Your wealth and honors are immense. Lavinia is not the only bride in Latium. Please, give up this dangerous match. If you fall, I have no ally left. And what would your father Daunus say?"
But Turnus's fever only grew. The medicine of words inflamed the wound. "Do not weep for me, my king. I am not afraid of death. Let me buy this peace with my blood if that is what fate demands."

Queen Amata, weeping and half-mad, clutched Turnus's hand. "If you have any love for me, do not fight Aeneas. If you die, I will not survive you. I will not live to see a Trojan son-in-law." Lavinia heard her mother's pleas, and tears ran down her burning cheeks.

A deep blush spread over Lavinia's face, like Indian ivory stained with crimson dye, or white lilies blushing among red roses. Turnus stared at her, and the sight only sharpened his desire for battle.

"Do not try to send me off with tears, mother. No one can postpone what is fated." He turned to the Rutulian herald: "Tell the Trojan I will meet him at dawn on the field between the armies. Let this war end between us two."

He called for his horses, those Thracian steeds that Orithyia had given to Pilumnus, whiter than snow, faster than the wind. He checked their harness while the grooms clapped their necks and combed their manes.
He buckled his armor of gold and mountain brass, fitted his sword and shield, and grasped the spear he had taken from the Auruncan fields, tempered and sharp. He shook it until it hummed.
From the great horse's nostrils, fire seemed to fly, and sparks fell from his stamping hooves. If only Turnus could match his boast with his fate.
Across the plain, Aeneas armed himself in his god-made steel and whetted his courage for the contest, glad that the war would end with this one fight.

The morning came. Both armies marched out and marked the field between the camps. They planted their spears, hung their shields on the turf, and left a wide space for the duel. From the walls, old men, mothers, and maidens watched.
The Latin legions came with bristling spears. The Trojans and Tuscans marched in full armor. The ground shook under the weight of so many feet. Neither army looked like men headed for peace.
When Turnus's sister Juturna, a river nymph beloved of Jupiter, saw the uneven match, she wept. She tore her hair and beat her breast. She knew her brother would die.

The two kings appeared in ceremony. Latinus rode in a four-horse chariot, his temples crowned with twelve golden rays like the Sun's. Turnus came in his own chariot drawn by white horses, gripping two broad-pointed spears.

Aeneas drew his shining sword and swore by the earth, the sea, the stars, and all the gods: "If Turnus wins, the Trojans will withdraw to Evander's city and never return. If I win, I will not make the Italians subjects of Troy. Let both nations live as equals under equal laws. I will bring the sacred rites. Latinus shall keep his throne."

Latinus stood before his own altar and swore by the same gods, by the rivers and the sea, by the powers above and below: "This peace shall hold forever, whatever comes. No force shall break it. As surely as this scepter will never sprout leaves again."

But the solemn treaty was watched with growing unease. The Rutulians thought Turnus outmatched. His thin frame, his pale color as he stepped forward, the inequality of the contest, all fed their fear.
The murmur spread through the ranks. Men looked at each other with doubt. They measured the two champions and found the balance tilting against their own.

Juturna saw her chance in the crowd's wavering mood. She disguised herself as the nobleman Camers and worked through the ranks, whispering: "Are you not ashamed to let one man die for you all? We outnumber them. Why not fight? The gods will favor the brave."

She crowned her deceit with a false omen. An eagle swooped down and snatched a swan from the river, but the flock of lesser birds rallied and chased the eagle until it dropped its prey. The Rutulians shouted that this was a sign from heaven.

The augur Tolumnius cried: "This is what I have prayed for! The gods show us the way. You are the small birds, and the Trojan is the eagle. Charge, and drive him back to sea!" He hurled his spear into the Trojan ranks. It struck one of nine brothers from Arcadia, a beautiful young man in his wedding armor. He fell, and the truce shattered.
The Latins surged forward. The Trojans surged to meet them. Aeneas shouted for his men to stop, that the treaty must hold, but an arrow struck him in the knee. He staggered and could fight no more.
Messapus spurred his horse at king Latinus's herald and struck him down. The field erupted into general battle. The sacred altars were overturned.
Messapus charged through the breaking lines, eager to destroy the peace. He trampled the old Tyrrhene Aulestes underfoot.
The Trojan priest Corynaeus grabbed a firebrand from the altar and burned Ebusus's face with it. The flames caught his beard and the stench of burning hair filled the air.
The fighting became a confused slaughter. Every man for himself, every weapon at hand.

Aeneas stumbled through the press, bareheaded and unarmed, his wounded knee bleeding. He shouted to his men that the truce was sacred, that he alone should fight. But a nameless arrow struck him and he could not stand.
An arrow had struck the prince. No one knew who fired it. Turnus saw Aeneas stagger and felt a surge of battle joy. He seized his spear and his horses and charged into the Trojan lines.

Turnus was transformed. He killed as he had never killed before. His chariot wheels rolled through blood. His horses' hooves trampled fallen bodies. He killed Sthenelus and Thamyris and Pholus with thrown spears, and the twin sons of Imbrasides from Lycia at close range.
Meanwhile Eumedes rallied the Trojans. Mnestheus drove back the Rutulian foot. Both sides fought with savage energy.
Turnus killed Dares, Butes, and Sybaris. He speared Chloreus and Sybaris through the face. Amycus fell to a stone. Turnus's horses trampled friend and foe alike.
Phegeus tried to stop Turnus's chariot by grabbing the bridle. He was dragged along until a spear-thrust pinned him to the chariot rail. His armor split and his body rolled under the wheels.
Back behind the lines, Aeneas was being treated by the healer Iapas, Apollo's own pupil. But no mortal art could reach the embedded arrow-point.
Iapas worked with practiced hands, probing the wound with forceps, but the arrowhead would not budge. Blood soaked the bandages. The noise of battle crept closer.
The old physician had tried herbs and honey and Apollo's own songs, but nothing worked. Aeneas stood propped on his spear, watching the battle rage, grinding his teeth in frustration.

But Venus, his divine mother, could not bear to watch. She flew to Mount Ida and gathered the herb dittany, which wild goats use to draw out arrows from their wounds. She steeped it in ambrosia and brought it unseen to the camp.

The healer touched the wound with the divine herb. Instantly, the pain stopped. The blood clotted. The arrow fell free into Iapas's hand without being pulled. "This is no mortal medicine," the old man said. "A god has healed you. Go to battle."

Aeneas embraced his son. "Learn from me, boy. When you are a man, remember your father's courage and your uncle Hector's example." He strode through the camp gate, fully armed, his divine shield blazing.
Now Turnus, posted on a hill, saw the Trojan army coming and felt his blood run cold. The Latins trembled.
Aeneas moved across the field like a thundercloud descending on the sea, as black swallows dart through palace halls, hunting flies.
Turnus could not find Aeneas in the press. His sister Juturna, disguised as his charioteer Metiscus, steered his horses away from the Trojan prince every time they drew near.
What could he do? He burned to fight, but every time he turned toward Aeneas, the chariot veered away. His mind was a whirl of frustration and shame.
What god can count the dead who fell that day? Turnus and Aeneas raged across the plain like two forest fires driven by opposing winds, burning everything they touched.
Aeneas killed Sucro, a Rutulian champion, with two strokes of his sword. He killed the twin brothers Amycus and Diores. He killed Talos, Tanais, and Cethegus in a single rush.
Three Trojans fell in quick succession, felled by a single charge from Turnus. He killed them without breaking stride.
Turnus slew the Lycian brothers sent from Apollo's shrine, and Paris's Menetes, who had been a simple fisherman before the war dragged him in.
Like twin fires on different sides of a forest, Turnus and Aeneas burned paths through the enemy ranks, meeting neither truce nor rest.
Turnus hurled a stone at Murranus and knocked him from his chariot. The horses trampled their master.
Hyllus charged Turnus face to face. Turnus smashed through his helmet with a spear that lodged in his brain.
Iolas fell, too, whom neither Greek arms nor great Achilles could kill at Troy. He had come so far only to die on Italian soil.

The Trojans heard their prince's command and charged the walls with renewed fury. Scaling ladders clattered against the stone. Grappling hooks bit into the parapets. The defenders fought hand to hand on the battlements, shoving ladders backward and hurling stones at the men below. But Aeneas's men kept coming, wave after wave, unstoppable as the tide.
Both armies were fully engaged now. The reserves, the wounded, the allies, all fought in one vast confused melee. The gods above looked down and pitied both sides.
Venus whispered to her son: "Leave the open battle. Storm the city. Once Latinus's capital falls, the war is over." Aeneas gathered his captains and pointed at the walls: "We end this now."
They formed a wedge and charged the walls. Ladders went up. Firebrands flew. The defenders on the towers fought back desperately, but Aeneas's men were unstoppable.
Inside the city, chaos reigned. Some demanded surrender. Others barred the gates. Women and old men screamed from the rooftops.
And now fate prepared its cruelest stroke.

When Queen Amata saw the Trojans scaling the walls and no sign of Turnus's army, she believed her champion was dead. Maddened by grief and guilt, she screamed that she was the cause of all this ruin. She tore her purple robe into a noose and hanged herself from a high beam.

When the news reached Turnus, racing through the distant fields, he pulled up his horses. His sister Juturna, still disguised as his driver, tried to keep him away from the city. But shouts and smoke rose from the walls. Turnus knew.

"Sister, I have known it was you since you took Metiscus's place. Do not try to save me any longer. Let me meet my fate. You cannot change what the gods have decided." Even as he spoke, a messenger galloped up: "Turnus! The city burns. Amata is dead. Latinus is locked in his palace. The Latins are throwing down their arms. Aeneas storms the walls. Only you can save us."

Turnus sat stunned, a thousand emotions warring in his face. Shame, grief, fury, and the madness of love burned in his eyes. When his reason cleared, he looked toward the burning city. Flames were licking the tower above the gate. "This is enough, sister. Fate calls, and I will answer. Let me fight Aeneas and die, if that is what the gods demand. You will not see your brother shamed."

He leaped from his chariot, sprinted through the enemy lines, and stood before the walls. "Stop!" he shouted to both armies. "The treaty stands. This fight is mine." Both sides drew back and opened a space.

Aeneas heard the shout and came striding from the burning gate. The two champions faced each other at last across the dusty plain. They were like two bulls charging in a mountain meadow, while the herd watches in silence to see who will rule.
Jupiter held up his golden scales and placed the fate of each man on a beam. He let go. One side sank down.

Turnus charged and hurled his great spear. But the weapon, though thrown with all his strength, only grazed Aeneas's shield. He stood amazed. When he reached for his sword, he found it was not the one his father had blessed but a brittle blade he had snatched up by mistake in the confusion of battle.

Turnus ran. Like a stag trapped between crimson hunting-nets and a raging river, he circled the field five times one way, five times the other. Aeneas chased him, wounded and slower, but relentless. Each time he closed in, Turnus swerved. Neither could rest. This was no game fought for a prize. They ran for Turnus's life and blood.

An ancient olive tree had stood in the center of the field, sacred to Faunus. The Trojans had cut it down to clear the ground. Aeneas's spear had lodged deep in its stump. He wrenched at it, but the root held fast. While he struggled, Juturna ran to her brother in the chariot-driver's form and gave him back his own true sword.
Venus, angered by the nymph's meddling, freed the spear from the stump. Both warriors stood fully armed again, one trusting sword, one trusting spear.
Jupiter spoke to Juno: "How long will you persist? Aeneas is destined for heaven. You know this. What is your purpose now?"

Juno answered, her pride broken at last: "I knew this. That is why I left the battlefield, though it cost me everything to do so. But grant me one thing: when peace is made, do not force the Latins to change their name or language. Let Troy perish forever as a name. Let the Latins remain Latins. Let the new race be Roman, not Trojan."

Jupiter smiled: "You are truly my sister, daughter of Saturn. No one nurses a grudge like you. Very well. The Trojans will merge with the Latins. They will keep Italian customs, the Italian tongue, and Italian dress. They will become one people, and the Romans who spring from them will honor the gods more faithfully than any nation on earth. You yourself will be pleased." Juno, satisfied at last, withdrew her hatred from the sky.

Jupiter then sent one of the twin Furies, the Dirae, down from heaven in the shape of a small screaming owl. It flew at Turnus's face, beating its wings against his shield. An unnatural chill crept through his veins. His voice froze. His hair stood on end.

Juturna recognized the omen. "What can I do for you now, brother? I am immortal, which means I must endure this grief forever. Death would be kinder. Without you, what light remains for me?" She covered her head with her green veil and plunged, weeping, into her river's depths.

Aeneas charged, shaking his huge spear like a battering ram. "No more running, Turnus. This is not a footrace. This is war. Transform yourself into anything you wish. Fly to the stars or hide in the earth. You will not escape."

Turnus looked around for help. He saw a massive ancient boundary stone, so heavy that twelve modern men could not lift it. He heaved it up in his trembling hands and hurled it at Aeneas. But his arms did not feel like his own. His knees buckled. The stone fell short and thudded harmlessly on the ground.

Like a man in a nightmare who tries to run but cannot, who strains every muscle but goes nowhere, Turnus stood paralyzed. A thousand thoughts flashed through his mind, but no escape, no help, no weapon offered itself.

Aeneas took careful aim, measured the distance with narrowed eyes, and hurled his spear with all his weight behind it. It flew like a siege engine's bolt, like black lightning. It burst through the edge of the great shield, through seven layers of hide and bronze, and into Turnus's thigh. The giant warrior crumpled and fell.

A groan went up from both armies. Turnus lay on the ground, his proud eyes raised to heaven, his right hand stretched out in supplication. "I have earned this," he said. "I do not beg for my life. Use your victory as you see fit. But if a father's grief can touch you, I beg you: send my body back to my people. You have won. Lavinia is your wife. The Latins have seen me beaten. Do not carry your hatred any further."

Aeneas stood over him with his sword drawn, and for a moment his arm hesitated. The words were moving him. He was on the very edge of mercy. Then his eyes fell on the belt Turnus wore, the belt stripped from young Pallas's body, gleaming with its familiar studs of gold. The sight hit him like a blow. His eyes blazed with fury and all pity vanished. "You stand there wearing the spoils of a boy I loved, and you ask me for mercy? It is Pallas who strikes this blow. Pallas who sacrifices you with this steel." He drove his sword to the hilt in Turnus's chest. The great body went limp. The proud spirit fled with an angry moan to the shades below.
